docs.title: Sanic RESTful Framework
docs.text: Welcome to Sanic RESTful Framework (SRF) — a powerful and flexible RESTful API development framework built on Sanic.

docs.title: What is SRF?
docs.text:
Sanic RESTful Framework (hereafter referred to as SRF) is a modern RESTful API development framework designed for Sanic applications. It provides a complete set of tools and best practices to help you quickly build high-performance web APIs.

SRF is inspired by Django REST framework (hereafter referred to as DRF), bringing its excellent design concepts to the asynchronous Sanic ecosystem. If you are familiar with DRF, you will be able to get started with SRF quickly. Even if you are not familiar with DRF, that is fine — SRF's convenience will certainly help you build your application quickly!

docs.title: Why choose SRF?
docs.text:
• 🚀 High performance: Built on Sanic, with outstanding performance
  • 📦 Common components: Provides authentication, permissions, pagination, filtering, rate limiting, and other foundational components
  • 🎯 Simple and easy to use: Offers an experience closest to Django REST Framework, with a gentle learning curve
  • 🔧 Flexible and extensible: Modular design makes customization and extension easy
  • 🔒 Security extension points: Provides JWT, permission, and rate limiting components; production security still requires application configuration and auditing
  • 📊 Ready out of the box: Provides health checks, exception handling, HTTP status codes, and other practical utilities

docs.title: ViewSet and routing
docs.text:
• Class-based view sets (ViewSet) that automatically generate RESTful routes
  • Supports standard CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete, List, etc.)
  • Easily add custom actions with the @action decorator
  • Automatic route discovery and registration

docs.title: Authentication and authorization
docs.text:
• JWT (JSON Web Token) authentication support
  • Social login integration (GitHub OAuth, etc.)
  • Flexible permission system (IsAuthenticated, SafeMethodOnly, SuperuserOnly, etc.)
  • Provides authentication middleware utilities that the application must wire in according to its routing strategy

docs.title: Data processing
docs.text:
• Data validation and serialization based on Pydantic
  • Page-number pagination and sorting

docs.title: Security features
docs.text:
• Rate limiting middleware (based on IP, user, path, etc.)
  • CSRF protection is implemented by the application according to its authentication approach
  • Password encryption (bcrypt)
  • Authentication keys must be configured explicitly by the application

docs.title: Quick preview
docs.text:
Here is a simple example showing how to create a RESTful API with SRF:

from sanic import Sanic
from srf.views import BaseViewSet
from srf.route import SanicRouter

from tortoise import fields
from tortoise.models import Model
from tortoise.contrib.sanic import register_tortoise
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


# Define the ORM model
class Product(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    name = fields.CharField(max_length=100)
    price = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)
    description = fields.TextField()


# Define the Schema model
class ProductSchema(BaseModel):
    id: int | None = None
    name: str
    price: float
    description: str
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)


# Define the ViewSet
class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    schema = ProductSchema

    @property
    def queryset(self):
        return Product.all()


# Create the application and routes
app = Sanic("MyApp")
register_tortoise(app, db_url=*, modules=*})
router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")
router.register("products", ProductViewSet)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

Once the routes are registered, these ViewSet endpoints are available:

  • GET /api/products - Get the product list
  • POST /api/products - Create a new product
  • GET /api/products/<pk> - Get a single product
  • PUT/PATCH /api/products/<pk> - Update a product
  • DELETE /api/products/<pk> - Delete a product

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
SRF reads configuration through srf.config.settings (LazySettings). The lookup order is:

  1. The app.config most recently bound via settings.set_app(app)
  2. The uppercase defaults defined in the srf.config.settings module

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
Set this up in your Sanic configuration:

from sanic import Sanic
from srf.config import settings

app = Sanic("MyApp")
settings.set_app(app)

LazySettings is a process-level singleton. When multiple applications share a single process, a later set_app() call affects all code that reads configuration through settings.

docs.title: Default configuration
docs.text: The following options are defined in srf/config/settings.py; the source code is authoritative.

docs.title: Pagination / Filtering / Permissions
docs.text:
Defaults used when a ViewSet does not declare the corresponding class attributes.

Option Default Description PAGINATION_CLASS PageNumberPagination Default pagination class DEFAULT_FILTERS [SearchFilter, QueryParamFilter, OrderingFactory, ...] Default filter chain DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES (AllowAny,) Default permission classes

docs.title: Serialization and caching
docs.text: Option Default Description BASE_DIR os.getcwd() Project root directory (process working directory) CACHE_ROOT BASE_DIR/.diskcache Cache directory DATETIME_FORMAT "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" Datetime string template JSON_ENCODER custom_dumps JSON serialization function (handles datetime / Exception); must be wired into Sanic by the application

docs.title: Health checks and rate limiting
docs.text:
The health check route actually reads app.config.HEALTH_CHECK_LIST:

from srf.health.checks import RedisCheck

app.config.HEALTH_CHECK_LIST = [RedisCheck]
app.ctx.redis = redis_client
Option Default Description HEALTH_CHECK_LIST [] List of health check classes REQUEST_LIMITERS [] List of rate limiters; throttle_rate() reads app.config.REQUEST_LIMITERS, falling back to settings.REQUEST_LIMITERS THROTTLE_REDIS_PREFIX "throttle" Redis key prefix for rate limiting (RedisStorage)

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
srf.tools.email.send_email() reads settings.EMAIL_CONFIG. LazySettings prefers app.config.EMAIL_CONFIG, so the application can override it at startup; when it is not overridden, srf.config.settings.EMAIL_CONFIG is used and its attributes are read from environment variables at module import time.

Attribute Environment variable Description EMAIL_CONFIG.from_email FROM_EMAIL Sender address EMAIL_CONFIG.smtp_server SMTP_SERVER SMTP server EMAIL_CONFIG.smtp_port SMTP_PORT SMTP port EMAIL_CONFIG.password PASSWORD Email password / authorization code

docs.title: Social login
docs.text:
See Social Login for a GitHub OAuth tutorial.

Option Default Description SOCIAL_CONFIG GitHub OAuth configuration dict Fields are read from environment variables such as GITHUB_CLIENT_ID SOCIAL_LOGIN_COOKIE_KEY "oauth_state" Cookie name for the OAuth state SOCIAL_LOGIN_COOKIE_KEY_MAX_AGE 600 State cookie lifetime (seconds)

docs.title: Registration verification codes and passwords
docs.text: Option Default Description MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH 8 Minimum password length USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_VERIFY_CODE_TTL 60 Verification code lifetime (seconds) USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_CODE "USER_REGISTER:EMAIL_CODE:{email}" Redis key template for verification codes USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_CODE_TIMES "USER_REGISTER:EMAIL_CODE_TIMES:{email}" Redis key template for failure counts USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_CODE_TIMES_LIMIT 10 Maximum number of verification failures

docs.title: JWT
docs.text:
JWT_SECRET (signing key) and SECRET_KEY (refresh token digest key) have no defaults and must be set explicitly in app.config. register_jwt_urls() converts JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRES to seconds and passes it to sanic-jwt.

Option Default Description JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRES timedelta(hours=24) Access token lifetime JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRES timedelta(days=30) Refresh token lifetime

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Separate sensitive information: use environment variables for secrets and passwords
  2. Multi-environment configuration: create different configurations for development, testing, and production
  3. Use a .env file: convenient for local development
  4. Do not commit .env: add .env to .gitignore
  5. Provide defaults: use the second argument of os.getenv() for default values
  6. Validate configuration: validate required options (such as JWT_SECRET) at application startup
  7. Document configuration: describe all options in the README

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Sanic RESTful Framework (SRF) provides a complete set of tools and features to help you quickly build high-quality RESTful APIs.

docs.title: 🎯 Class-based view sets (ViewSet)
docs.text:
ViewSet is the core concept of SRF. It provides an elegant way to organize and manage API endpoints.

Features:

  • Automatically generates standard RESTful routes
  • Built-in basic CRUD view functions (Create, Read, Update, Delete, List)
  • Supports the Mixin pattern for flexible composition of functionality
  • Easily add custom route view functions with the @action decorator
  • Fast development with an experience close to Django REST Framework

Advantages:

  • Reduces duplicated code and improves development efficiency
  • Consistent code style and structure
  • Easy to test and maintain

docs.title: 🎨 Automatic route generation
docs.text:
SanicRouter automatically generates routes for ViewSets:

Standard routes:

  • GET /api/resource → list
  • POST /api/resource → create
  • GET /api/resource/<pk> → retrieve
  • PUT/PATCH /api/resource/<pk> → update
  • DELETE /api/resource/<pk> → destroy

Custom routes:

  • Defined with the @action decorator
  • Automatically discovered and registered
  • Supports both collection-level and detail-level actions

docs.title: 🔐 Authentication components
docs.text:
SRF provides multiple authentication methods to meet the needs of different scenarios.

Supported authentication methods:

  • JWT authentication: Stateless authentication based on JSON Web Tokens
  • Social login: Supports GitHub OAuth (other platforms can be extended)
  • Email verification: Built-in email verification code functionality

Authentication features:

  • Provides token validation middleware (wired in by the application)
  • Permission control through built-in and custom permission classes
  • Password storage with encryption (bcrypt)
  • The JWT secret must be configured explicitly by the application; authentication middleware is wired in by the application

docs.title: 🛡️ Flexible permission system
docs.text:
A class-based permission system that supports view-level and object-level permission control.

Built-in permission classes:

  • AllowAny: Always allow (the default when permission_classes is not declared)
  • IsAuthenticated: The user must be logged in
  • SuperuserOnly: The user must be a superuser
  • SafeMethodOnly: Only safe HTTP methods are allowed (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS)
  • Implement custom permission control based on BasePermission

docs.title: Data validation and serialization
docs.text:
• Data validation based on Pydantic
  • Automatic data serialization and deserialization
  • Supports separating read and write schemas
  • Type-safe and IDE-friendly

docs.title: Filtering system
docs.text:
SRF provides multiple filters that can be combined:

  1. SearchFilter: Keyword containment matching on fields configured in search_fields
  2. QueryParamFilter: Exact filtering based on query parameters
  3. OrderingFactory: Sorting functionality
  4. And more...

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
• Page-number-based pagination
  • The page size can be set via a query parameter (maximum 100)
  • Returns a unified paginated response format

docs.title: 🚦 Rate limiting middleware
docs.text:
Protect your API from abuse with multiple rate limiting strategies:

  • IPRateLimit: Rate limiting based on IP address
  • UserRateLimit: Rate limiting based on user ID
  • PathRateLimit: Rate limiting based on request path plus user/IP
  • HeaderRateLimit: Rate limiting based on request headers

Storage backends:

  • In-memory storage (MemoryStorage)
  • Redis storage (RedisStorage)

docs.title: 🏥 Health checks
docs.text:
Built-in health check functionality to monitor the status of the application and its dependencies. Register the check classes to run via the HEALTH_CHECK_LIST configuration.

Built-in service checks:

  • RedisCheck (Redis)
  • SQLiteCheck (SQLite)

Features:

  • Runs the configured checks and returns a status mapping
  • The response remains HTTP 200 even when a check fails
  • Easy to integrate into monitoring systems

docs.title: 📝 Audit events
docs.text: SRF provides an Event model, EventSchema, and a superuser-only EventViewSet for creating, listing, and reading events. Events must be written by the application itself; the framework does not automatically record every request.

docs.title: HTTP status codes
docs.text:
• Enums for common HTTP status codes
  • Semantic constant names (such as HTTP_200_OK, HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND)

docs.title: Exception handling
docs.text:
• Converts some exceptions within ViewSets
  • Custom exception classes
  • Global unified responses require the application to register Sanic exception handlers

docs.title: Email sending
docs.text:
• Synchronous SMTP based on the standard library smtplib (srf/tools/email.py)
  • send_email(to_email, subject, content) sends HTML content emails (synchronous)
  • send_template_email(...) provides asynchronous template email sending, executing SMTP in a thread internally
  • Registration verification codes default to six digits and support Redis TTL and failure-count limits

docs.title: Convention over configuration
docs.text: SRF follows the principle of "convention over configuration", providing sensible defaults so you can start developing quickly. At the same time it remains highly configurable, letting you customize any behavior when needed.

docs.title: Modular and extensible
docs.text: SRF is modular by design: every feature is an independent module that you can use as needed. It also provides clear extension points for adding custom functionality.

docs.title: Type safety
docs.text: Through Pydantic and type annotations, SRF provides good type safety, reducing runtime errors and improving code quality.

docs.title: Async first
docs.text: SRF fully leverages Python's asyncio features and Sanic's asynchronous architecture to deliver high-performance API services.

docs.title: Performance advantages
docs.text:
• Asynchronous I/O: Built on Sanic with native async/await support
  • Efficient routing: Routes are generated and registered automatically, reducing runtime overhead
  • Modular: Components are wired in as needed; data caching is left to the application
  • Lightweight: A lean core with modules loaded on demand

docs.title: A mature ecosystem
docs.text: • Built on Sanic as the foundation, it integrates seamlessly with frameworks across the ecosystem

docs.title: IDE-friendly
docs.text:
• Complete type annotations
  • Clear code structure
  • Good code hints and autocompletion

docs.title: Easy to test
docs.text:
• Class-based design facilitates unit testing
  • Clear interfaces and separation of responsibilities
  • Supports mocking and dependency injection

docs.title: Well documented
docs.text:
• Detailed documentation in multiple languages
  • Rich code examples
  • API reference documentation

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
SRF is suitable for the following scenarios:

  • ✅ Building RESTful API services
  • ✅ Applications that require high concurrency
  • ✅ Microservice architectures
  • ✅ Projects with separated frontend and backend
  • ✅ Mobile application backends
  • ✅ IoT platforms
  • ✅ Data API services

docs.title: v0.1.3
docs.text:
Routing, pagination and rate limiting fixes; auth API split

  • Fixed HEAD requests returning 405, synchronous @action returning 500, and GitHub login without id
  • Pagination falls back and clamps invalid parameters; empty results report page 1
  • Redis rate limiting increments and expires keys atomically via Lua
  • Auth route registration split into register_jwt_urls() and friends; added change-password / reset-password
  • Health check module moved to srf.health.route; email config can be overridden via app.config.EMAIL_CONFIG
  • English and Chinese docs synced; added tests/test_jwt_flow.py

docs.title: v0.1.1

  • Added the asynchronous template email interface send_template_email().
  • GitHub OAuth login now uses a one-time login code flow.

docs.title: API Reference: Exceptions
docs.text:
All public exceptions in SRF inherit from Sanic's HTTPException and are converted into JSON responses by Sanic. See Exceptions for usage.

from srf.exceptions import (
    ImproperlyConfigured,
    PydanticValidationException,
    TargetObjectAlreadyExist,
    TooManyRequest,
)

docs.title: Exceptions at a glance
docs.text:
Exception Status code Typical trigger TargetObjectAlreadyExist 409 A unique constraint is violated on create; it can also be raised explicitly in custom update logic PydanticValidationException 422 Pydantic or Tortoise ValidationError ImproperlyConfigured 500 An option has an invalid type (for example, INSTALLED_APPS is not a list) TooManyRequest 429 Too many failed verification code attempts (for example, repeated confirmations on register)

TargetObjectAlreadyExist, PydanticValidationException and TooManyRequest set quiet = True, so Sanic does not log the corresponding request as an error.

docs.title: Exception conversion in ViewSets
docs.text:
GenericAPIView.as_view() wraps view methods and performs the following conversions:

Original exception Conversion result pydantic.ValidationError PydanticValidationException → 422 tortoise.exceptions.ValidationError PydanticValidationException → 422 tortoise.exceptions.IntegrityError CreateModelMixin.perform_create() converts it to TargetObjectAlreadyExist → 409

UpdateModelMixin.perform_update() does not catch IntegrityError itself; to turn unique constraint conflicts into 409, catch it in a subclass (see UserViewSet.perform_update) and raise TargetObjectAlreadyExist.

Sanic built-in exceptions such as NotFound, Forbidden, BadRequest, and MethodNotAllowed keep their original status codes and are not wrapped.

The response body is generated by Sanic's JSONRenderer:

{
  "description": "Unprocessable Entity",
  "status": 422,
  "message": "..."
}

docs.title: API Reference: Filters
docs.text:
Filters convert query parameters into Tortoise Q expressions or filter() calls. ListModelMixin.list() runs them in the order of filter_class. See Filtering for usage.

from srf.filters import (
    JsonLogicFilter,
    OrderingFactory,
    QueryParamFilter,
    SearchFilter,
)

docs.title: Default filters and parameters
docs.text:
settings.DEFAULT_FILTERS has the order SearchFilter, JsonLogicFilter, QueryParamFilter, OrderingFactory, so the following parameters can be used together:

Parameter Filter Purpose search SearchFilter Fuzzy search across multiple fields filter JsonLogicFilter JSON Logic expressions ordering OrderingFactory Sorting Any key in filter_fields QueryParamFilter Exact matching

The field allowlists come from ViewSet class attributes:

from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class BookViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    search_fields = ["title", "author"]
    # alias -> ORM field
    filter_fields = {"published": "is_published", "author_id": "author__id"}
    ordering_fields = ["create_time", "title"]

Lists are treated as "the field name is the parameter name", while dictionaries map external parameter names to internal ORM fields.

docs.title: Filter classes
docs.text:
All four built-in filters inherit from BaseFilter and declare the allowlist fields they need through class attributes.

Subclasses must set cls_fields (the name of the ViewSet attribute that stores the field allowlist); otherwise a TypeError is raised at class definition time. filter_fields is normalized at instantiation into a {field: ORM field} dictionary.

Semantics of ?search=alice admin:

  • Split into multiple keywords by whitespace;
  • Each keyword is matched across all fields with OR (__icontains);
  • Multiple keywords are combined with AND.

?filter= accepts a JSON Logic expression. Supported operators:

Operator Meaning Generated query == Equals field=value != / ! Not equals NOT field=value > Greater than field__gt >= Greater than or equal field__gte < Less than field__lt <= Less than or equal field__lte in In field__in not in Not in NOT field__in like Contains field__icontains

Combination rules:

  • The arguments of and / or are an array of expressions;
  • The argument of not is a single expression;
  • Fields must appear in filter_fields; otherwise the condition is ignored;
  • If the JSON cannot be parsed, 400 Bad Request is returned.
# ?filter=<urlencoded JSON>
{
    "and": [
        {"==": [{"var": "published"}, True]},
        {"like": [{"var": "title"}, "python"]},
    ]
}

Parameter names must exactly match the keys of filter_fields:

  • Single value: ?published=true → exact match;
  • Repeated parameter: ?id=1&id=2 → id__in=[1, 2].

Parameters not in the allowlist are ignored and do not raise an error.

?ordering=-create_time,title: comma-separated; a - prefix means descending. Fields not present in ordering_fields are ignored; if all fields are invalid, the default order is kept.

docs.title: BaseFilter
docs.text:
BaseFilter(view_class)

Bases: ABC

Base class for all filters.

Subclasses must set cls_fields to the name of the view attribute holding the field configuration (e.g. "search_fields"); missing it raises TypeError at class-definition time.

Attributes:

Name Type Description cls_fields str | None

Name of the view attribute that lists the allowed fields.

view_class

The view instance this filter is bound to.

filter_fields

docs.title: API Reference: Pagination
docs.text:
Pagination behavior is determined by the ViewSet's pagination_class, which defaults to PageNumberPagination. See Pagination for usage.

from srf.paginator import PageNumberPagination
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class BookViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    queryset = Book.all()  # Tortoise QuerySet
    schema = BookSchema  # Pydantic model
    pagination_class = PageNumberPagination

docs.title: Response structure
docs.text:
The object returned by list() always contains four fields:

{
  "count": 42,
  "next": true,
  "previous": false,
  "results": [{ "id": 1, "title": "..." }]
}

Differences from DRF

next / previous are booleans, not URLs to the next/previous page. The frontend must construct page numbers itself.

docs.title: Query parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Rule page 1 Falls back/clamps to 1 when it is not an integer or is less than 1 page_size 10 Falls back to 10 when it is not an integer, clamps to 1 when below 1, and is limited to MAX_PAGE_SIZE (default 100)
  • When the page number exceeds the total number of pages, an empty results is returned and count is still the total record count.
  • The upper bound of page_size is controlled by the MAX_PAGE_SIZE class attribute, which subclasses can override; the constructor also clamps page / page_size to valid ranges.
  • The parameter names are controlled by PAGE_QUERY_PARAM / PAGE_SIZE_QUERY_PARAM.

docs.title: API Reference: Permissions
docs.text:
Permission classes run before each request enters a view method. See Permissions and API Permissions for usage.

from srf.permission import IsAuthenticated, SuperuserOnly

docs.title: Permission contract
docs.text:
Permission class methods are defined as static methods; the framework calls them directly on the class and does not instantiate it:

from sanic import Request


class IsOwner:
    @staticmethod
    def has_permission(request: Request, view=None) -> bool:
        return getattr(request.ctx, "user", None) is not None

    @staticmethod
    def has_object_permission(request: Request, view=None, obj=None) -> bool:
        user = getattr(request.ctx, "user", None)
        return user is not None and obj.user_id == user.id
  • Both synchronous and asynchronous (async def) methods are supported; the framework automatically awaits coroutine results.
  • A falsy return value raises 403 Forbidden.
  • Because methods are called on the class, permission classes cannot rely on instance state stored in __init__; data that must be shared across methods should be placed on class attributes or request.ctx.

When object-level permissions are checked

has_object_permission() is only called inside get_object(), so it only applies to retrieve / update / destroy. list does not check object permissions per item; filter by user in get_queryset() instead. create also performs no object-level checks.

docs.title: Using in a ViewSet
docs.text:
from your_py import IsOwner
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class ProfileViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    queryset = User.all()
    schema = UserSchema
    permission_classes = (IsOwner,)

docs.text:
Class has_permission behavior AllowAny Always allow (default permission) IsAuthenticated request.ctx.user exists and is_active is true SafeMethodOnly Only safe methods are allowed: GET / HEAD / OPTIONS SuperuserOnly request.ctx.user exists and is_superuser is true

When permission_classes is not declared, settings.DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES is used, which defaults to (AllowAny,).

permission_classes can be any iterable; each element must provide has_permission(request, view), and optionally has_object_permission(request, view, obj) when object-level permissions are needed.

docs.title: API Reference: Routing
docs.text:
The routing layer exposes a single public class, SanicRouter: it splits a ViewSet into collection routes, detail routes, and @action routes, then registers them on a Sanic application or Blueprint. See Routing for usage.

from srf.route import SanicRouter

router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="/api/v1")
router.register("books", BookViewSet)

options: heading_level: 3 members: - init - register show_source: false inherited_members: false

docs.text:
SanicRouter(instance: Sanic | Blueprint, prefix: str = '')

DRF-style router that registers a ViewSet as collection/detail routes on a Sanic app or Blueprint, and auto-discovers @action methods.

Route names follow {name}-list, {name}-detail and {name}-{url_name}.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default instance Sanic | Blueprint

Sanic app or Blueprint to register routes on.

required prefix str

Optional URL prefix, e.g. "api" produces /api/<path>.

''

docs.text: prefix = f'/{strip('/')}' if prefix else ''

docs.title: instance instance-attribute
docs.text: instance = instance

docs.title: register
docs.text:
register(
    path: str,
    view_cls: type[GenericAPIView],
    name: str | None = None,
) -> None

Register view_cls under path.

Only implemented actions get routes: GET/POST {path} map to list/create, GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE {path}/<pk> map to retrieve/update/update/destroy. Methods decorated with @action are discovered and registered automatically.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str

Resource path, e.g. "books".

required view_cls type[GenericAPIView]

The ViewSet class to register.

required name str | None

Route name prefix; defaults to path.

None

docs.title: Registration result
docs.text:
register(path, view_cls, name=None) only registers routes for view methods that actually exist on the class:

URL HTTP View method Route name {prefix}/{path} GET list {name}-list {prefix}/{path} HEAD list {name}-list {prefix}/{path} POST create {name}-list {prefix}/{path}/<pk> GET retrieve {name}-detail {prefix}/{path}/<pk> HEAD retrieve {name}-detail {prefix}/{path}/<pk> PUT update {name}-detail {prefix}/{path}/<pk> PATCH update {name}-detail {prefix}/{path}/<pk> DELETE destroy {name}-detail {prefix}/{path}/{url_path} action.methods Method decorated with action {name}-{url_name} {prefix}/{path}/<pk>/{url_path} action.methods Action with detail=True {name}-{url_name}
  • name defaults to path.
  • If a ViewSet does not define list, no collection route is created; the same applies to detail routes.
  • GET routes also support HEAD, reusing the same list / retrieve method.
  • A read-only ViewSet generates only the routes for list / retrieve (including HEAD).

docs.title: Discovery rules for @action
docs.text:
register() uses inspect.getmembers() to scan the view class (including inherited methods); any method with an extra_info attribute is registered as a separate route. extra_info is written by action:

Parameter Default Purpose detail False When True, the URL includes <pk> methods ("GET",) HTTP methods accepted by the action url_path "/{function name}" Appended after the collection/detail path url_name Function name Used to build the route name {name}-{url_name}

Prefix normalization

prefix="api/v1/" is normalized to /api/v1, and leading/trailing / in path are removed. Therefore SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/v1").register("/books/", BookViewSet) produces the collection URL /api/v1/books.

Duplicate route names

SanicRouter does not check for route name conflicts. If two ViewSets use the same name, or two actions use the same url_name, you must ensure uniqueness yourself; otherwise Sanic reports a duplicate route name.

docs.title: API Reference: Views
docs.text:
The view layer is the core of request handling in SRF. GenericAPIView handles action dispatch, schema validation, permissions, filtering, and pagination, while several CRUD mixins combine into ready-to-use ViewSets. For mechanism details and complete examples, see ViewSet and Actions and Decorators.

from srf.views import BaseViewSet, GenericAPIView, ReadOnlyModelViewSet, action

docs.title: Action dispatch
docs.text:
as_view(actions) maps HTTP methods to view methods. Usually SanicRouter.register() builds the mapping automatically; you only need to pass it yourself when calling app.add_route() manually:

from sanic import Sanic

from srf.views import BaseViewSet

app = Sanic("demo")


class BookViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    queryset = Book.all()  # Tortoise QuerySet
    schema = BookSchema  # Pydantic model


app.add_route(
    BookViewSet.as_view({"get": "list", "post": "create"}),
    "/books",
)

The keys of actions are lowercase HTTP methods and the values are the method names to call. Methods not present in the mapping are not registered as routes; if the corresponding method cannot be resolved at runtime, 405 Method Not Allowed is raised.

PUT and PATCH

Currently both put and patch map to update, and update validates the request body against the full schema. The semantic distinction between the two (full update / partial update) has not been implemented yet.

docs.title: View base classes
docs.text:
GenericAPIView is the common base class for all views; the other three composite classes simply pre-assemble the CRUD mixins.

Differences between the three composite classes:

Class Provided actions BaseViewSet create / list / retrieve / update / destroy ReadOnlyModelViewSet list / retrieve CreateAndReadOnlyModelViewSet create / list / retrieve

docs.title: GenericAPIView
docs.text:
GenericAPIView(*args, **kwargs)

Bases: HTTPMethodView

Base class for all SRF views: schema validation, permissions, filtering and pagination.

Attributes:

Name Type Description schema type[BaseModel] | None

Pydantic model class used to validate request data and serialize responses. Set it on the subclass or override get_schema().

queryset QuerySet | None

Tortoise QuerySet the view operates on. Set it on the subclass or override get_queryset().

filter_class list[type[BaseFilter]]

Filter classes applied in list(). Defaults to settings.DEFAULT_FILTERS when not declared on the class.

permission_classes Iterable[type[BasePermission]]

Permission classes checked before the handler runs. Defaults to settings.DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES.

pagination_class type[BasePagination]

Pagination class used by list(). Defaults to settings.PAGINATION_CLASS.

search_fields list[str] | dict[str, str]

Fields matched by SearchFilter via ?search= (icontains). Accepts a list of ORM field names or a dict of {alias: orm_field}.

filter_fields list[str] | dict[str, str]

Fields allowed for exact filtering by QueryParamFilter / JsonLogicFilter. Accepts a list or a dict of {param: orm_field}.

ordering_fields list[str] | dict[str, str]

Fields allowed for ordering via ?ordering=. Use -name for descending order.

docs.title: get_schema
docs.text:
get_schema() -> type[BaseModel]

Return the Pydantic model class for this view action.

Override this method (or set class attribute schema) like DRF's get_serializer_class / serializer_class. Uses self.action and self.request set by as_view — do not pass request as a parameter.

docs.title: normalize_pk
docs.text:
normalize_pk(pk, model: type[Model] | None = None)

Coerce the route parameter pk to the model's pk type before it reaches a query.

Sanic always hands <pk> over as str. Querying with the raw str only works by implicit conversion, and a non-integer pk against an int field raises ValueError deep inside Tortoise (a 500). Convert up front: a pk that cannot be parsed can never match a row, so respond 404.

Check view-level permissions. Permission classes are used as callables on the class (no instantiation). Supports both sync and async has_permission().

Check object-level permissions. Permission classes are used as callables on the class (no instantiation). Supports both sync and async has_object_permission().

docs.title: as_view classmethod
docs.text:
as_view(actions: dict[str, str] | None = None)

Construct a view function for registering with Sanic.

actions maps an HTTP method to a view method, for example `{"get": "list"}or{"get": "retrieve"}. Callers pass this map explicitly:SanicRouter.registerbuilds it, andadd_routecallers pass it themselves. Sanic's default route method is GET; that does not chooselistversusretrieve``.

docs.title: BaseViewSet
docs.text:
BaseViewSet(*args, **kwargs)

Bases: GenericAPIView, ModelMixin

Full-featured ViewSet: all five CRUD actions plus schema validation, permissions, filtering and pagination from GenericAPIView.

docs.title: ReadOnlyModelViewSet
docs.text:
ReadOnlyModelViewSet(*args, **kwargs)

Bases: GenericAPIView, ListModelMixin, RetrieveModelMixin

Read-only ViewSet exposing only list and retrieve.

docs.title: CreateAndReadOnlyModelViewSet
docs.text:
CreateAndReadOnlyModelViewSet(*args, **kwargs)

Bases: GenericAPIView, CreateModelMixin, ListModelMixin, RetrieveModelMixin

ViewSet exposing create, list and retrieve — no update or delete.

docs.title: CRUD mixins
docs.text:
Each mixin provides a single action; inherit from them directly when you need finer-grained composition.

Behavior of create:

  • Returns 400 when the request body is not JSON.
  • Validates input with schema using strict=True, then calls perform_create().
  • Serializes output with the same schema and returns 201.
  • Database unique constraint violations (IntegrityError) are converted to 409 TargetObjectAlreadyExist.

When looking up an object, the primary key type is normalized first, then object-level permission checks run; if the object does not exist, 404 is returned.

perform_update() only writes fields explicitly provided in the request (exclude_unset=True) and skips primary key fields.

Returns 204 No Content after a successful delete.

The execution order of list is: get_queryset() → filter_queryset() → pagination_class.from_queryset() → paginate(). See Pagination for the response structure.

docs.title: Action decorator
docs.text:
action declares a regular method in a ViewSet as a standalone endpoint; SanicRouter discovers and registers it automatically.

validate_request is used to decorate functional views (for example, register and verify_email in srf.auth). Request validation for ViewSets is handled uniformly by as_view(), so there is no need to stack this decorator on top.

docs.title: action
docs.text:
action(
    *,
    detail: bool = False,
    methods: Sequence[str] = ("GET",),
    url_path: str | None = None,
    url_name: str | None = None,
    **kwargs
) -> Callable

Mark a method as a viewset action.

:param methods: List of HTTP methods allowed for this action :param detail: If True, action requires a pk parameter. If False, action is on collection. :param url_path: Custom URL path for this action, default to be the name of the method :param url_name: Custom URL name for this action, default to be the name of the method

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide walks you through creating your first Sanic RESTful Framework project from scratch.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Before you begin, make sure your environment meets the following requirements:

  • Python: 3.11 or later
  • pip: Python package manager
  • Database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, etc. (this tutorial uses SQLite)

docs.title: 1. Create the project directory
docs.text:
mkdir bookstore
cd bookstore

docs.title: 2. Create a virtual environment
docs.text:
Using conda to create an isolated Python environment is recommended:

# Create a virtual environment named srf
conda create -n srf python=3.11

# Activate the virtual environment
conda activate srf

Or use UV:

uv init

docs.title: 3. Install SRF
docs.text:
pip install sanic-restful-framework
# or
uv add sanic-restful-framework

docs.title: 4. Check the runtime dependencies
docs.text:
Installing SRF automatically installs the core dependencies, including Sanic >=25.0.0,<26, Tortoise ORM >=1.1.8,<2, Pydantic >=2.6.1,<3, sanic-jwt, redis, and bcrypt.

sanic-cors and python-dotenv are optional dependencies, used for CORS integration and loading configuration from .env files respectively; install them separately only when using the corresponding examples.

docs.title: Create your first project
docs.text: Let's create a simple book management API.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the application file
docs.text:
Create an app.py file:

from sanic import Sanic
from tortoise.contrib.sanic import register_tortoise
from srf.config import settings

# Create the Sanic application
app = Sanic("BookStore")

# Configure SRF
settings.set_app(app)

# Database configuration
register_tortoise(
    app,
    db_url="sqlite://db.sqlite3",
    modules={"models": ["models"]},
    generate_schemas=True,
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, debug=True)

docs.title: Step 2: Define the data model
docs.text:
Create a models.py file:

from tortoise import fields
from tortoise.models import Model


class Book(Model):
    """Book model"""

    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    title = fields.CharField(max_length=200)
    author = fields.CharField(max_length=100)
    price = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)
    stock = fields.IntField(default=0)

    class Meta:
        table = "books"

docs.title: Step 3: Define the schemas
docs.text:
Create a schemas.py file:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ConfigDict
from typing import Optional


class BookSchemaWriter(BaseModel):
    """Book write schema (used for create and update)"""

    title: str = Field(..., max_length=200)
    author: str = Field(..., max_length=100)
    price: float = Field(..., gt=0)
    stock: int = Field(default=0, ge=0)


class BookSchemaReader(BaseModel):
    """Book read schema (used for serialization)"""

    id: int
    title: str
    author: str
    price: float
    stock: int

    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)

docs.title: Step 4: Create the ViewSet
docs.text:
Create a viewsets.py file:

from srf.views import BaseViewSet
from srf.views.decorators import action
from sanic.response import json
from models import Book
from schemas import BookSchemaWriter, BookSchemaReader


class BookViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    """Book ViewSet"""

    search_fields = ["title", "author"]
    # Both search_fields and filter_fields support alias mapping; dictionaries map query parameter names to ORM fields
    filter_fields = {"author": "author"}

    @property
    def queryset(self):
        return Book.all()

    def get_schema(self):
        # as_view sets self.action; distinguish read/write schemas by ViewSet action name here.
        if self.action in ("list", "retrieve"):
            return BookSchemaReader
        return BookSchemaWriter

    @action(methods=["get"], detail=False, url_path="search")
    async def search_books(self, request):
        """Search books"""
        keyword = request.args.get("q", "")
        books = await Book.filter(title__icontains=keyword)
        data = [BookSchemaReader.model_validate(b).model_dump() for b in books]
        return json({"results": data})

docs.title: Step 5: Register the routes
docs.text:
Add the imports at the top of app.py, then register the ViewSet after register_tortoise(...):

from srf.route import SanicRouter
from viewsets import BookViewSet

router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")
router.register("books", BookViewSet, name="books")

SanicRouter automatically generates collection routes (/api/books) and detail routes (/api/books/<pk>) for the ViewSet, and discovers @action methods.

docs.title: Step 6: Run the application
docs.text:
python app.py

You should see output similar to the following:

[2026-02-07 10:00:00 +0800] [12345] [INFO] Goin' Fast @ http://0.0.0.0:8000
[2026-02-07 10:00:00 +0800] [12345] [INFO] Starting worker [12345]

docs.title: Test the API
docs.text: Your API is now running. Let's test it!

docs.title: 1. Create a book
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/books \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "title": "Python Programming",
    "author": "John Doe",
    "price": 89.00,
    "stock": 50
  }'

Response:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Python Programming",
  "author": "John Doe",
  "price": 89.00,
  "stock": 50
}

docs.title: 2. Get the book list
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:8000/api/books

Response:

{
  "count": 1,
  "next": false,
  "previous": false,
  "results": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "title": "Python Programming",
      "author": "John Doe",
      "price": 89.00,
      "stock": 50
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: 3. Get a single book
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:8000/api/books/1

The response body is the same book object returned by the create endpoint.

docs.title: 4. Update a book
docs.text:
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8000/api/books/1 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "title": "Python Programming (2nd Edition)",
    "author": "John Doe",
    "price": 99.00,
    "stock": 50
  }'

Response:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Python Programming (2nd Edition)",
  "author": "John Doe",
  "price": 99.00,
  "stock": 50
}

docs.title: 5. Filter by field
docs.text:
Parameters declared in filter_fields can be used directly for exact filtering:

curl "http://localhost:8000/api/books?author=John%20Doe"

The response structure is the same as the list endpoint, with only matching records in results.

docs.title: 6. Pagination
docs.text:
# Get page 1 with 10 items per page
curl "http://localhost:8000/api/books?page=1&page_size=10"

The response format is the same as above: count is the total, and results contains the current page's data.

docs.title: 7. Use a custom action
docs.text:
# The custom action uses the q parameter to search titles
curl "http://localhost:8000/api/books/search?q=Python"

Response:

{
  "results": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "title": "Python Programming (2nd Edition)",
      "author": "John Doe",
      "price": 99.00,
      "stock": 50
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: 8. Delete a book
docs.text:
curl -i -X DELETE http://localhost:8000/api/books/1

Response: 204 No Content (no response body).

docs.title: Complete project structure
docs.text:
bookstore/
├── app.py                 # Application entry point
├── models.py              # Data models
├── schemas.py             # Pydantic schemas
├── viewsets.py            # ViewSets
└── db.sqlite3             # Database file (generated automatically)

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
Congratulations! You have successfully created your first SRF project. Next you can:

  1. Add authentication: see Authentication to add JWT authentication to your API
  2. Add permission control: read Permissions to restrict user access
  3. Learn more about ViewSets: study the advanced usage of Views
  4. Configure the project: see Project Setup for more configuration options

docs.title: How do I change the database?
docs.text:
Change db_url in register_tortoise:

# PostgreSQL
db_url = "postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/dbname"

# MySQL
db_url = "mysql://user:password@localhost:3306/dbname"

# SQLite
db_url = "sqlite://db.sqlite3"

docs.title: How do I disable automatic schema generation?
docs.text:
Set generate_schemas=False:

register_tortoise(
    app,
    db_url="sqlite://db.sqlite3",
    modules={"models": ["models"]},
    generate_schemas=False,  # Disable automatic generation
)

docs.title: How do I change the port?
docs.text:
Change the arguments to app.run():

app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=9000, debug=True)

docs.title: How do I enable CORS?
docs.text:
Install and configure sanic-cors:

pip install sanic-cors

from sanic_cors import CORS

app = Sanic("BookStore")
CORS(app)

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text: This chapter explains how to properly set up and configure an SRF project, including project structure, configuration management, database setup, and more.

docs.title: Recommended project structure
docs.text:
Assume an SRF project is structured as follows:

myproject/
├── app.py                      # Application entry point
├── config.py                   # Configuration file
├── requirements.txt            # Dependency list
├── .env                        # Environment variables
├── models/                     # Data models
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── product.py
│   ├── order.py
│   └── category.py
├── schemas/                    # Pydantic schemas
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── product.py
│   ├── order.py
│   └── category.py
├── viewsets/                   # ViewSets
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── product.py
│   ├── order.py
│   └── category.py
├── routes.py                   # Route configuration
├── permissions.py              # Custom permission classes
├── filters.py                  # Custom filters
├── middleware.py               # Custom middleware
├── utils/                      # Utility functions
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── helpers.py
│   └── validators.py
└── tests/                      # Tests
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── test_products.py
    └── test_orders.py

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Create a .env file to store sensitive information:

# .env
SECRET_KEY=your-secret-key-here
DATABASE_URL=sqlite://db.sqlite3
REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/0

# JWT configuration
JWT_SECRET=your-jwt-secret
# Access/refresh token lifetimes are defined as timedelta in srf.config.settings and are not read from environment variables

# Email configuration (the names actually read by srf.tools.email)
FROM_EMAIL=your-email@gmail.com
SMTP_SERVER=smtp.gmail.com
SMTP_PORT=587
PASSWORD=your-password

docs.title: Configuration file
docs.text:
Create config.py to manage configuration:

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

# Load environment variables
load_dotenv()

class Config:
    """Base configuration"""
    SECRET_KEY = os.getenv("SECRET_KEY", "your-secret-key")
    DATABASE_URL = os.getenv("DATABASE_URL", "sqlite://db.sqlite3")
    REDIS_URL = os.getenv("REDIS_URL", "redis://localhost:6379/0")

    # JWT configuration
    JWT_SECRET = os.getenv("JWT_SECRET", SECRET_KEY)
    # JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRES is defined as a timedelta in srf.config.settings;
    # register_jwt_urls converts it to seconds and passes it to sanic-jwt

    # Email: send_email reads settings.EMAIL_CONFIG; app.config.EMAIL_CONFIG can override it.
    # Defaults come from the FROM_EMAIL/SMTP_SERVER/SMTP_PORT/PASSWORD environment variables.

    # Social login (uppercase key names, consistent with SOCIAL_CONFIG)
    SOCIAL_CONFIG = {
        "github": {...}
    }

    # CORS configuration
    CORS_ORIGINS = ["http://localhost:3000", "http://localhost:8080"]

class DevelopmentConfig(Config):
    """Development environment configuration"""
    DEBUG = True
    DATABASE_URL = "sqlite://db_dev.sqlite3"

class ProductionConfig(Config):
    """Production environment configuration"""
    DEBUG = False
    DATABASE_URL = os.getenv("DATABASE_URL")

class TestConfig(Config):
    """Test environment configuration"""
    TESTING = True
    DATABASE_URL = "sqlite://:memory:"

# Select configuration based on the environment variable
config_map = {
    "development": DevelopmentConfig,
    "production": ProductionConfig,
    "test": TestConfig,
}

env = os.getenv("ENVIRONMENT", "development")
config = config_map[env]

python-dotenv is not a dependency of SRF; install it separately if you want to load configuration from a .env file:

pip install python-dotenv

docs.title: Applying configuration
docs.text:
Apply the configuration in app.py:

from sanic import Sanic
from tortoise.contrib.sanic import register_tortoise
from srf.config import settings
from config import config

app = Sanic("MyApp")

# Apply configuration to Sanic
app.config.update_config(config)

# Configure SRF
settings.set_app(app)

# Configure the database
register_tortoise(
    app,
    db_url=config.DATABASE_URL,
    modules={"models": ["models"]},
    generate_schemas=True,
)

docs.text:
from tortoise.contrib.sanic import register_tortoise

register_tortoise(
    app,
    config={
        "connections": {
            "default": {
                "engine": "tortoise.backends.asyncpg",
                "credentials": {
                    "host": "localhost",
                    "port": 5432,
                    "user": "postgres",
                    "password": "password",
                    "database": "mydb",
                    "minsize": 1,
                    "maxsize": 5,
                },
            }
        },
        "apps": {
            "models": {
                "models": ["models"],
                "default_connection": "default",
            }
        },
        "use_tz": False,
        "timezone": "Asia/Shanghai",
    },
    generate_schemas=True,
)

docs.title: Database migrations
docs.text:
Tortoise ORM 1.1.8 and later include a migration CLI. First define a complete TORTOISE_ORM configuration in config.py:

TORTOISE_ORM = {
    "connections": {"default": "sqlite://db.sqlite3"},
    "apps": {
        "models": {
            "models": ["models"],
            "default_connection": "default",
        }
    },
}

Use the Tortoise CLI in the project root to initialize the migration directory and manage migrations:

# Initialize the migration directory for the models app
tortoise -c config.TORTOISE_ORM init models

# Generate a migration after model changes
tortoise -c config.TORTOISE_ORM makemigrations models --name add_products

# Apply migrations
tortoise -c config.TORTOISE_ORM migrate

# Roll back the most recent migration
tortoise -c config.TORTOISE_ORM downgrade

config.TORTOISE_ORM after -c is the dotted path to the Python module and configuration variable; the model module names and migration app names in the configuration should match the project structure. Small examples in development can use generate_schemas=True to create tables automatically; production environments should manage schema changes through migrations.

docs.title: JWT and route registration (recommended)
docs.text:
Prefer register_all_auth_urls: it initializes JWT (login /me /verify /refresh) and registers registration, logout, email verification, and social login routes in one call:

from srf.auth.route import register_all_auth_urls

register_all_auth_urls(app, prefix="/api/auth")

If you only need a subset, call register_jwt_urls (JWT endpoints only; requires a Sanic app instance), register_auth_urls (register/verify_email/logout), or register_social_auth_urls (GitHub OAuth) separately. To customize sanic-jwt parameters, call sanic_jwt.Initialize directly.

docs.title: Authentication middleware
docs.text:
from srf.middleware.authmiddleware import set_user_to_request_ctx

app.middleware("request")(set_user_to_request_ctx)

By default (strict=False) a request with no token falls back to AnonymousUser; pass strict=True for mandatory authentication, or filter public endpoints with a whitelist first. See Authentication Middleware for details.

docs.title: Rate limiting middleware
docs.text:
from srf.middleware.throttlemiddleware import (
    MemoryStorage,
    IPRateLimit,
    UserRateLimit,
    throttle_rate,
)

# Create storage
storage = MemoryStorage()

# Configure rate limiting rules
app.config.REQUEST_LIMITERS = [
    IPRateLimit(100, 60, storage),      # IP: 100 requests/minute
    UserRateLimit(1000, 60, storage),   # User: 1000 requests/minute
]


@app.middleware("request")
async def throttle_middleware(request):
    """Rate limiting middleware"""
    if not await throttle_rate(request):
        from sanic.response import json

        return json({"error": "Too many requests, please try again later"}, status=429)

docs.title: CORS middleware
docs.text:
sanic-cors is an optional dependency and is not installed with SRF. Install it first if you need this integration:

pip install sanic-cors

from sanic_cors import CORS

# Configure CORS
CORS(
    app,
    origins=config.CORS_ORIGINS,
    methods=["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"],
    allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type"],
    expose_headers=["Content-Range", "X-Content-Range"],
    supports_credentials=True,
)

docs.title: Basic route registration
docs.text:
Create routes.py:

from srf.route import SanicRouter
from viewsets.product import ProductViewSet
from viewsets.order import OrderViewSet
from viewsets.category import CategoryViewSet


def register_routes(app):
    """Register all routes"""
    router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")

    # Register ViewSets
    router.register("products", ProductViewSet, name="products")
    router.register("orders", OrderViewSet, name="orders")
    router.register("categories", CategoryViewSet, name="categories")

Call it in app.py:

from routes import register_routes

app = Sanic("MyApp")
# ... other configuration ...

# Register routes
register_routes(app)

# Configure logging
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO if not config.DEBUG else logging.DEBUG,
    format="%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s",

docs.title: Exception handling
docs.text:
from sanic.exceptions import NotFound, InvalidUsage
from sanic.log import logger
from srf.views.http_status import HTTPStatus
from sanic.response import json


@app.exception(NotFound)
async def handle_not_found(request, exception):
    """Handle 404 errors"""
    return json({"error": "Resource not found", "message": str(exception)}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND)


@app.exception(InvalidUsage)
async def handle_invalid_usage(request, exception):
    """Handle 400 errors"""
    return json({"error": "Invalid request", "message": str(exception)}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST)


@app.exception(Exception)
async def handle_exception(request, exception):
    """Handle uncaught exceptions"""
    logger.error(f"Unhandled exception: {exception}", exc_info=True)
    return json({"error": "Internal server error"}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)

docs.title: Complete application example
docs.text:
app.py:

from sanic import Sanic
from sanic_cors import CORS
from tortoise.contrib.sanic import register_tortoise
from srf.auth.route import register_all_auth_urls
from srf.config import settings
from srf.health.route import health_check
from srf.middleware.authmiddleware import set_user_to_request_ctx
from config import config
from routes import register_routes
import logging

# Create the application
app = Sanic("MyApp")

# Apply configuration
app.config.update_config(config)
settings.set_app(app)

# Configure CORS
CORS(app, origins=config.CORS_ORIGINS)

# Configure logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

# Register the database
register_tortoise(
    app,
    db_url=config.DATABASE_URL,
    modules={"models": ["models"]},
    generate_schemas=True,
)


# Register middleware (optional auth by default: no token -> AnonymousUser,
# strict=True for mandatory authentication)
app.middleware("request")(set_user_to_request_ctx)


# Register routes
register_routes(app)
register_all_auth_urls(app, prefix="/api/auth")
app.add_route(health_check, "/health", methods=["GET"])


# Exception handling
@app.exception(Exception)
async def handle_exception(request, exception):
    from sanic.response import json

    logging.error(f"Error: {exception}", exc_info=True)
    return json({"error": str(exception)}, status=500)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(
        host=getattr(config, "HOST", "0.0.0.0"),
        port=getattr(config, "PORT", 8000),
        debug=config.DEBUG,
        auto_reload=config.DEBUG,
    )

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Use environment variables: do not hard-code sensitive information in code
  2. Separate configuration: create different configurations for different environments
  3. Use migrations: manage database changes through migrations
  4. Logging: log important operations and errors
  5. Exception handling: handle exceptions globally and return friendly error messages
  6. Health checks: provide a health check endpoint for monitoring systems
  7. Rate limiting: protect the API from abuse
  8. CORS configuration: configure cross-origin access correctly

docs.title: Other Features
docs.text: SRF provides many practical advanced features to help you build more robust and fully featured API services.

docs.title: Feature overview
docs.text: This chapter covers the following advanced features:

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• Health Checks: Monitor the health of the application and its dependencies
  • Exception Handling: Built-in ViewSet conversions and global Sanic handling recommendations
  • HTTP Status: Standardized status code management

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text:
• Authentication Middleware: Automatically handle user authentication
  • CSRF Middleware: Prevent cross-site request forgery attacks
  • Rate Limiting Middleware: Prevent API abuse and control request frequency

docs.title: Essential for production
docs.text:
The following features are strongly recommended for production environments:

  1. Health checks: integrate into monitoring systems to know the service status in real time
  2. Rate limiting middleware: prevent malicious requests and DDoS attacks
  3. Exception handling: provide friendly error messages without exposing internal details
  4. Authentication middleware: automatically handle user authentication

docs.title: Helpful in development
docs.text:
The following features help with debugging in development environments:

  1. HTTP status codes: use semantic constants for more readable code
  2. Exception handling: quickly locate problems and provide detailed error information

docs.title: Feature combination examples
docs.text: For a complete application skeleton that combines configuration, authentication middleware, routing, health checks, and exception handling, see Project Setup; for how to integrate rate limiters, see Rate Limiting Middleware.

docs.title: Monitoring and logging
docs.text: For basic logging configuration, see Project Setup. The following only covers request/response-level monitoring.

docs.title: Request logging middleware
docs.text:
@app.middleware("request")
async def log_request(request):
    """Log request information"""
    logger.info(f"{request.method} {request.path} from {request.ip}")


@app.middleware("response")
async def log_response(request, response):
    """Log response information"""
    logger.info(f"{request.method} {request.path} -> {response.status}")

docs.title: Performance monitoring
docs.text:
import time


@app.middleware("request")
async def add_start_time(request):
    """Record the request start time"""
    request.ctx.start_time = time.time()


@app.middleware("response")
async def add_process_time(request, response):
    """Calculate the processing time"""
    if hasattr(request.ctx, "start_time"):
        process_time = time.time() - request.ctx.start_time
        response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = str(process_time)

Production environments must use HTTPS:

from sanic.log import logger
from sanic.response import json


# Configure SSL
app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=443, ssl={"cert": "/path/to/cert.pem", "key": "/path/to/key.pem"})

docs.text: app.config.REQUEST_MAX_SIZE = 10 * 1024 * 1024  # 10MB

app.config.RESPONSE_TIMEOUT = 60

app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, debug=False)

@app.exception(Exception)
async def handle_exception(request, exception):

    logger.error(f"Error: {exception}", exc_info=True)

    # Return only a generic error to the client

docs.title: 5. Validate input
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator


class ProductSchema(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float

    @field_validator("price")
    @classmethod
    def validate_price(cls, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Price must be greater than 0")
        if value > 1000000:
            raise ValueError("Price cannot exceed 1,000,000")
        return value

docs.title: 2. Use caching
docs.text:
from redis.asyncio import Redis, ConnectionPool


@app.before_server_start
async def setup_redis(app, loop):
    pool = ConnectionPool.from_url("redis://localhost:6379", max_connections=10)
    app.ctx.redis = Redis(connection_pool=pool)


# Use caching in a ViewSet
class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def retrieve(self, request, pk):
        # Try to get it from the cache
        redis = request.app.ctx.redis
        cache_key = f"product:{pk}"
        cached = await redis.get(cache_key)

        if cached:
            from sanic.response import json
            import json as json_lib

            return json(json_lib.loads(cached))

        # Get it from the database
        obj = await self.get_object(pk)
        schema = self.get_schema()
        data = schema.model_validate(obj).model_dump(mode="json")

        # Store it in the cache (expires in 10 minutes)
        await redis.setex(cache_key, 600, json_lib.dumps(data))

        from sanic.response import json

        return json(data)

Caching and object permissions

The example above reads the cache before calling get_object(), so a cache hit skips object-level permission checks. Endpoints that need object-level permissions should perform permission checks first, or set cache keys scoped to the user.

docs.text:
import asyncio


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def create(self, request):
        # Run multiple asynchronous operations in parallel
        results = await asyncio.gather(Product.all().count(), Category.all(), Brand.all())

        product_count, categories, brands = results

docs.title: Exception Handling
docs.text: SRF defines several exception classes and, inside GenericAPIView.as_view(), converts Pydantic / Tortoise validation errors into 422 exceptions. It does not install a global unified exception handler.

docs.title: SRF exceptions
docs.text:
from srf.exceptions import ImproperlyConfigured, PydanticValidationException, TargetObjectAlreadyExist, TooManyRequest
  • TargetObjectAlreadyExist: An HTTPException subclass with status code 409 (quiet=True).
  • ImproperlyConfigured: An HTTPException subclass with status code 500.
  • PydanticValidationException: An HTTPException subclass with status code 422 (quiet=True).
  • TooManyRequest: An HTTPException subclass with status code 429 (quiet=True), raised when verification code attempts exceed the limit.

They only define status codes and have no custom JSON response structure; the final response format is decided by Sanic's default exception handling (or handlers registered by the application).

docs.title: Built-in ViewSet handling
docs.text:
as_view() only catches two kinds of validation errors in the try block around the handler call:

Exception Handling pydantic.ValidationError Converted to PydanticValidationException (422), with message str(error) tortoise.exceptions.ValidationError Same as above, converted to 422

Apart from these two kinds, as_view() does not catch other exceptions:

  • Sanic NotFound (404) raised by get_object() is passed directly to Sanic.
  • Any HTTPException raised inside the handler (such as BadRequest, Forbidden) is also passed directly to Sanic.
  • check_permissions() runs before the try block, and the Forbidden it raises is likewise handled by Sanic.

For example:

from sanic.exceptions import BadRequest
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def create(self, request):
        if request.json is None:
            raise BadRequest("The request body cannot be empty")
        # ...

docs.title: Special CRUD behavior
docs.text:
• get_object() uses get_or_none() and raises Sanic NotFound when the object does not exist or the primary key cannot be parsed.
  • perform_create() converts Tortoise IntegrityError into a 409 TargetObjectAlreadyExist(message="data conflict").
  • When the request JSON is None, the built-in create/update return an empty 400 response directly.

docs.title: Global unified responses
docs.text:
If the application needs a consistent format, register a Sanic exception handler:

from sanic.exceptions import HTTPException
from sanic.response import json


@app.exception(HTTPException)
async def handle_http_exception(request, exception):
    return json(
        {
            "error": type(exception).__name__,
            "message": getattr(exception, "message", str(exception)),
        },
        status=exception.status_code,
    )

Note: the PydanticValidationException produced by as_view() is also an HTTPException, so it reaches this global handler; the application can use that to output a unified format.

In production you can add a fallback handler, but do not expose stack traces to clients:

from sanic.log import error_logger


@app.exception(Exception)
async def handle_unexpected_error(request, exception):
    error_logger.exception("Unhandled exception")
    return json(
        {"error": "INTERNAL_ERROR", "message": "Internal server error"},
        status=500,
    )

docs.title: Pydantic errors
docs.text:
The built-in response currently uses str(error). If clients need structured field errors, you can return error.errors() in a custom ViewSet handler, or modify the framework's capture logic:

except ValidationError as error:
    return JSONResponse(
        {"errors": error.errors(include_url=False)},
        status=422,
    )

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Classify exceptions: use different exception classes for different kinds of errors
  2. Friendly error messages: provide clear, helpful error messages
  3. Unified response format: use a consistent error response structure
  4. Log details: log contextual information about errors
  5. Hide internal details: do not expose internal errors in production
  6. Use appropriate status codes: use the correct HTTP status code for different errors
  7. Internationalization: support error messages in multiple languages

docs.text:
• Study HTTP Status to learn about using status codes
  • Read Authentication to learn about authentication exceptions
  • See Views to learn about exception handling in ViewSets

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text: SRF provides built-in health check functionality for monitoring the status of the application and its dependencies.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Health checks are an important part of monitoring systems. They can:

  • Detect whether the application is running normally
  • Monitor the availability of dependent services (databases, caches, etc.)
  • Integrate with load balancers and container orchestration systems
  • Provide early warning so problems are found in time

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Redis is already included in SRF's dependencies; aiosqlite, used by the SQLite check, is an optional dependency and requires pip install aiosqlite.

docs.title: 1. Register the health check route and configure the check list
docs.text:
The route reads app.config.HEALTH_CHECK_LIST (an empty list by default) and runs each check class in it once.

from sanic import Sanic
from srf.health.checks import RedisCheck, SQLiteCheck
from srf.health.route import health_check

app = Sanic("MyApp")
app.config.HEALTH_CHECK_LIST = [RedisCheck, SQLiteCheck]
app.add_route(health_check, "/health", methods=["GET"])

docs.title: 2. Configure the dependent services
docs.text:
Check classes read clients from app.ctx by name. The Redis check uses app.ctx.redis; the SQLite check requires app.ctx.sqlite to be an aiosqlite.Connection.

from aiosqlite import connect
from redis.asyncio import Redis


@app.before_server_start
async def setup_services(app):
    app.ctx.redis = Redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379/0")
    app.ctx.sqlite = await connect("db.sqlite3")

docs.title: 3. Access the health check endpoint
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:8000/health

The response is a JSON mapping from check names to statuses, for example:

{ "redis": "up", "sqlite": "down" }

Even when a check returns "down", the current handler still returns HTTP 200. If the client has not been mounted on app.ctx in advance, constructing the check instance raises an exception, which Sanic handles.

docs.title: Built-in health checks
docs.text: SRF provides the following check classes.

docs.title: RedisCheck
docs.text:
from srf.health.checks import RedisCheck
from redis.asyncio import Redis

app.ctx.redis = Redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379/0")

The check logic calls ping(), with a default timeout of 5 seconds.

docs.title: SQLiteCheck
docs.text:
from srf.health.checks import SQLiteCheck
from aiosqlite import connect

app.ctx.sqlite = await connect("db.sqlite3")

The check logic executes SELECT 1. This check requires aiosqlite; the standard library synchronous sqlite3.Connection cannot be used.

docs.title: Custom health checks
docs.text:
Subclass BaseHealthCheck, set name, implement check(), and add the check class to HEALTH_CHECK_LIST. On construction the framework reads app.ctx.<name> and sets it as an instance attribute with the same name. run() returns (name, "up") when the check succeeds, and logs the failure and returns (name, "down") when it fails.

from srf.health.checks import BaseHealthCheck


class APIServiceCheck(BaseHealthCheck):
    name = "api_service"
    timeout = 5

    async def check(self):
        await self.api_service.ping()


# The application initializes and creates the API client
app.ctx.api_service = api_client
app.config.HEALTH_CHECK_LIST = [APIServiceCheck]

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
from sanic import Sanic
from redis.asyncio import Redis
from aiosqlite import connect
from srf.health.checks import RedisCheck, SQLiteCheck
from srf.health.route import health_check

app = Sanic("MyApp")
app.config.HEALTH_CHECK_LIST = [RedisCheck, SQLiteCheck]
app.add_route(health_check, "/health", methods=["GET"])


@app.before_server_start
async def setup_services(app):
    app.ctx.redis = Redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379/0")
    app.ctx.sqlite = await connect("db.sqlite3")


@app.after_server_stop
async def cleanup_services(app):
    await app.ctx.redis.aclose()
    await app.ctx.sqlite.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=8000)

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Checks should complete quickly and have reasonable timeouts.
  2. Checks should avoid side effects.
  3. Only add dependencies that need monitoring to HEALTH_CHECK_LIST.
  4. Initialize the clients that checks depend on at application startup and close them on shutdown.
  5. If a load balancer needs a non-200 failure status, wrap health_check at the application layer and implement the appropriate status code.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Learn about Exception Handling to handle health check exceptions
  • Study Rate Limiting to protect the health check endpoint
  • See HTTP Status to learn about using status codes

docs.title: HTTP Status
docs.text: SRF provides enums for common HTTP status codes, making it convenient to use semantic constants in code.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Benefits of using status code constants:

  • Readability: HTTP_200_OK is clearer than 200
  • Type safety: avoid mistyping status codes
  • IDE support: provides autocompletion and documentation hints
  • Consistency: teams use consistent status codes

docs.title: Import
docs.text: from srf.views.http_status import HTTPStatus

docs.title: 1xx - Informational responses
docs.text:
Status code Constant Description 100 HTTP_100_CONTINUE Continue 101 HTTP_101_SWITCHING_PROTOCOLS Switching protocols 
from srf.views.http_status import is_informational

# Check whether it is an informational response
if is_informational(status_code):
    print("Informational response")

docs.title: 2xx - Successful responses
3xx - Redirects
4xx - Client errors
5xx - Server errors
Checking status code categories
docs.text:
from srf.views.http_status import (
    is_informational,
    is_success,
    is_redirect,
    is_client_error,
    is_server_error,
)

# Whether it is an informational response (1xx)
is_informational(100)  # True

# Whether it is a successful response (2xx)
is_success(200)  # True
is_success(201)  # True

# Whether it is a redirect (3xx)
is_redirect(301)  # True

# Whether it is a client error (4xx)
is_client_error(400)  # True
is_client_error(404)  # True

# Whether it is a server error (5xx)
is_server_error(500)  # True
is_server_error(503)  # True

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from sanic.exceptions import NotFound
from sanic.response import HTTPResponse, json
from srf.views import BaseViewSet
from srf.views.http_status import HTTPStatus


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def create(self, request):
        """Create a product"""
        # Validate the data
        schema_class = self.get_schema()
        try:
            schema = schema_class.model_validate(request.json, strict=True)
        except Exception as e:
            return json({"error": str(e)}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST)

        # Check whether it already exists
        if await Product.filter(sku=schema.sku).exists():
            return json({"error": "SKU already exists"}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_409_CONFLICT)

        # Create
        obj = await Product.create(**schema.model_dump(by_alias=False))

        # Serialize
        data = schema_class.model_validate(obj, from_attributes=True).model_dump(mode="json")

        # Return 201 Created
        return json(data, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_201_CREATED)

    async def destroy(self, request, pk):
        """Delete a product"""
        # Get the object
        try:
            obj = await self.get_object(pk)
        except NotFound:
            return json({"error": "Product not found"}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND)

        # Delete
        await obj.delete()

        # Return 204 No Content
        return HTTPResponse(status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)

docs.title: Custom actions
docs.text:
from srf.views.decorators import action


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    @action(methods=["post"], detail=True, url_path="publish")
    async def publish(self, request, pk):
        """Publish a product"""
        # Get the product
        try:
            product = await self.get_object(pk)
        except NotFound:
            return json({"error": "Product not found"}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND)

        # Check the status
        if product.is_published:
            return json({"error": "Product already published"}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_409_CONFLICT)

        # Publish
        product.is_published = True
        await product.save()

        return json({"message": "Published successfully"}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_200_OK)

docs.title: Standard RESTful API responses
docs.text: Operation Method Success status code Failure status codes List GET 200 OK 400 Bad Request Detail GET 200 OK 404 Not Found Create POST 201 Created 400 Bad Request, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity Update PUT/PATCH 200 OK 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 422 Unprocessable Entity Delete DELETE 204 No Content 404 Not Found

docs.title: Asynchronous tasks
docs.text:
@action(methods=["post"], detail=False, url_path="import")
async def import_products(self, request):
    """Bulk import products (asynchronous task)"""
    file = request.files.get("file")

    if not file:
        return json({"error": "Missing file"}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST)

    # Create an asynchronous task
    task_id = await create_import_task(file)

    # Return 202 Accepted
    return json({
        "message": "Task created",
        "task_id": task_id,
        "status_url": f"/api/tasks/{task_id}"
    }, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_202_ACCEPTED)

docs.title: Conditional requests
docs.text:
async def retrieve(self, request, pk):
    """Get a product (with conditional request support)"""
    product = await self.get_object(pk)

    # Check If-None-Match
    etag = f'"{product.id}-{product.updated_at.timestamp()}"'
    if_none_match = request.headers.get("If-None-Match")

    if if_none_match == etag:
        # Not modified
        return json({}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_304_NOT_MODIFIED)

    # Return the data
    schema = self.get_schema()
    data = schema.model_validate(product).model_dump()

    response = json(data, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_200_OK)
    response.headers["ETag"] = etag
    return response

docs.title: Complete constant list
docs.text: See HTTP Status API for the complete list of HTTPStatus enum members.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Use semantic constants: use HTTP_200_OK instead of 200
  2. Choose status codes correctly: use the appropriate status code for each situation
  3. Consistency: teams should use a consistent status code standard
  4. Documentation: describe the status codes of each endpoint in the API documentation
  5. Client-friendly: provide clear error messages and status codes
  6. Follow RESTful conventions: follow standard REST API status code conventions

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
# Return 200 for all errors
return json({"error": "not found"}, status=200)

# Use magic numbers
return json(data, status=201)

# Wrong status code
# Return 200 instead of 204 on successful delete
return json({"message": "deleted"}, status=200)

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
from sanic.response import HTTPResponse

# Use semantic constants
return json(data, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_201_CREATED)

# Use the appropriate status code
if not found:
    return json({"error": "not found"}, status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND)

# Return 204 on successful delete
return HTTPResponse(status=HTTPStatus.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)
