docs.text:
• Study Exception Handling to learn about the relationship between exceptions and status codes
  • Read Views to learn about using status codes in ViewSets
  • See the HTTP Status API for the complete constant list

docs.title: Authentication Middleware
docs.text:
The authentication middleware reads the JWT from the request and writes the user object from the database into request.ctx.user. authenticate_request() supports two modes:

  • strict=False (default, optional authentication): a request with no credentials at all (no Authorization header) resolves to request.ctx.user = AnonymousUser() (see srf.auth.models.AnonymousUser). A presented token that is malformed, invalid, expired, forged, or whose user no longer exists still raises 401 — once the client attempts authentication, the attempt must succeed.
  • strict=True (mandatory authentication): every request must carry a valid, non-expired access token; anything else (including requests with no credentials at all) raises 401.

Public endpoints (login, register, refresh, health checks, ...) can alternatively be filtered out by the caller BEFORE the function runs (whitelist), so they skip authentication entirely.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from srf.middleware.authmiddleware import set_user_to_request_ctx


@app.middleware("request")
async def auth_middleware(request):
    # Filter the whitelist first: public endpoints skip authentication entirely
    if request.path == "/health" or request.path.startswith("/api/auth/"):
        request.ctx.user = None
        return
    await set_user_to_request_ctx(request, strict=True)  # mandatory authentication

The application must provide the same secret used to issue tokens:

app.config.JWT_SECRET = "read from a secure environment variable"

docs.title: Request flow
docs.text:
1. Extract the token from Authorization: Bearer <token>. A missing header: strict=True raises 401, otherwise the request falls back to request.ctx.user = AnonymousUser(). A malformed header always raises 401.
  2. Verify the signature and expiry via request.app.ctx.auth; an expired, forged, or undecodable token raises 401 (in both modes).
  3. Call retrieve_user(request, payload) to load the user and put the ORM user into request.ctx.user; a missing or disabled user raises 401.

Note: whitelisted paths skip authentication entirely — even with a valid token, request.ctx.user stays None.

docs.title: extract_bearer_token
docs.text:
from srf.middleware.authmiddleware import extract_bearer_token

token = extract_bearer_token(request)

This function requires the authentication scheme to be Bearer (case-insensitive), and raises 401 when the request header is missing or malformed.

docs.title: authenticate_request
docs.text:
from srf.middleware.authmiddleware import authenticate_request

await authenticate_request(request)               # optional auth (default): no token -> AnonymousUser
await authenticate_request(request, strict=True)  # mandatory auth: no token -> 401
user = request.ctx.user

docs.title: set_user_to_request_ctx
docs.text: This function passes its arguments through to authenticate_request and can be used as application middleware. strict=False (default) is optional authentication: no credentials fall back to AnonymousUser; strict=True is mandatory authentication. A presented-but-invalid token always raises 401 in both modes (see authenticate_request).

docs.title: Middleware order
docs.text:
If user rate limiting, access logging, or similar logic needs to read request.ctx.user, make sure the authentication middleware runs first. The authentication context may not have been set yet, so read it with:

user = getattr(request.ctx, "user", None)

docs.title: Security limitations
docs.text:
• Every request with a valid token queries the database.
  • The authentication middleware itself does not implement a token blacklist; refresh tokens are managed by the authentication routes.

Production applications can configure token revocation and appropriate user caching as needed.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Authentication to configure token issuance.
  • Read Permissions to control the scope of user access.
  • Read Rate Limiting to protect authentication endpoints.

docs.title: CSRF Middleware
docs.text: SRF's CSRF protection is implemented by the application integrating Sanic middleware or another suitable component. When browsers make write requests using automatically attached cookie authentication, appropriate SameSite, Secure, and HttpOnly attributes should be set. When tokens are sent explicitly with Authorization: Bearer ..., traditional CSRF risk is lower, but CORS, XSS protection, and token storage still need to be configured correctly.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text: SRF provides rate limiting components in srf.middleware.throttlemiddleware, which the application integrates as needed.

docs.title: Component overview
docs.text:
• Rate limiters: IPRateLimit, UserRateLimit, PathRateLimit, HeaderRateLimit, all inheriting BaseRateLimit(limit, window, storage, scope=None); limit / window must be positive integers. A custom limiter only needs to implement get_key(request).
  • Storage: MemoryStorage (single-process sliding window, suitable only for development) and RedisStorage (fixed window usable across processes). Both implement an atomic allow(); rejected requests do not increase the counter.
  • Key dimensions: PathRateLimit includes the user or IP in its key; HeaderRateLimit hashes the header value and falls back to the IP when the header is missing. Limiters with different limit / window use different keys and do not pollute each other.
  • Entry point: throttle_rate(request) calls allow(request) on each limiter in app.config.REQUEST_LIMITERS in order, and rejects the request as soon as any returns falsy; when nothing is configured, no rate limiting is applied. On rejection, request.ctx.throttle_retry_after holds the suggested Retry-After value in seconds.

docs.title: Integration example
docs.text:
from sanic.response import json
from srf.middleware.throttlemiddleware import IPRateLimit, MemoryStorage, throttle_rate

storage = MemoryStorage()
app.config.REQUEST_LIMITERS = [
    IPRateLimit(limit=100, window=60, storage=storage),
]


@app.middleware("request")
async def throttle_middleware(request):
    if not await throttle_rate(request):
        return json(
            {"error": "Too many requests"},
            status=429,
            headers={"Retry-After": str(request.ctx.throttle_retry_after)},
        )

docs.title: Usage notes
docs.text:
• MemoryStorage is not shared across processes; use RedisStorage for multi-worker deployments.
  • User-level rate limiting depends on request.ctx.user, so the authentication middleware must run before the throttle middleware. Register them in this order:
@app.middleware("request")
async def auth_middleware(request):
    await set_user_to_request_ctx(request, strict=False)

@app.middleware("request")
async def throttle_middleware(request):
    if not await throttle_rate(request):
        return json({"error": "Too many requests"}, status=429)

In the opposite order, UserRateLimit treats every request as anonymous and degrades to IP-based limiting.

  • IP source: when Sanic's PROXIES_COUNT / REAL_IP_HEADER is configured, request.remote_addr (the real client IP) is used; otherwise the socket peer request.ip is used. SRF adds no extra proxy configuration.
  • Allowlists, metrics, and similar features must be extended by the application.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Authentication Middleware to confirm middleware order.
  • Read Health Checks to configure the monitoring endpoint.

docs.title: Authentication and Permissions Together
docs.text: Authentication is responsible for writing the current user into request.ctx.user, while permissions decide whether that user may access the ViewSet. See Permissions for complete documentation of permission classes and how object-level permissions are wired; this article only explains how the two combine, to avoid duplicating the permission reference.

docs.title: Basic configuration
docs.text:
from srf.middleware.authmiddleware import set_user_to_request_ctx
from srf.permission.permission import IsAuthenticated
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


@app.middleware("request")
async def auth_middleware(request):
    await set_user_to_request_ctx(request)


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    permission_classes = (IsAuthenticated,)

Before a request enters the ViewSet, BaseViewSet.check_permissions() calls has_permission(request, view) on the class (without instantiating it). It raises Forbidden on failure. The authentication middleware supports two modes: by default a request with no token falls back to AnonymousUser; strict=True enforces mandatory authentication — see Authentication Middleware. Both AnonymousUser (is_active=False) and None (whitelisted paths that skip authentication) are rejected by IsAuthenticated (403).

docs.title: Setting permissions by HTTP method
docs.text: To differentiate permissions by operation, simply override check_permissions(); see Permissions: Setting permissions by request method for the full approach (the permission reference page has a complete example).

docs.title: Object-level permissions
docs.text:
BaseViewSet.check_object_permissions() calls has_object_permission(request, view, obj) on the class. get_object() triggers this check, so retrieve / update / destroy as well as custom actions that explicitly call get_object() all run it. Use @staticmethod for custom object permissions:

from models import Order
from srf.permission.permission import BasePermission, IsAuthenticated
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class IsOwner(BasePermission):
    @staticmethod
    def has_object_permission(request, view=None, obj=None):
        return obj.user_id == request.ctx.user.id


class OrderViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    permission_classes = (IsAuthenticated, IsOwner)

The list endpoint still needs to limit visible data by filtering the queryset.

docs.title: Custom actions
docs.text: All actions first run the ViewSet's global check_permissions(); when additional checks are needed inside an action, follow the "Permissions for custom actions" section in Permissions.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Custom permissions should use @staticmethod, with the signatures has_permission(request, view=None) / has_object_permission(request, view=None, obj=None).
  • Object visibility for list endpoints still needs to be scoped via get_queryset() (or queryset).

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: SRF provides login and token generation through sanic-jwt, and provides a separate request middleware that validates the Bearer token, loads the user, and writes it to request.ctx.user.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before enabling JWT, set JWT_SECRET in the Sanic configuration (there is no longer a requirement to set the SECRET_KEY environment variable before import):

from sanic import Sanic
from srf.config import settings

app = Sanic("MyApp")
app.config.JWT_SECRET = "read from a secure environment variable"
app.config.SECRET_KEY = "read from another secure environment variable"
settings.set_app(app)

JWT_SECRET is used for JWT signing; SECRET_KEY is used to compute the HMAC digest of refresh tokens, and the database stores only the digest, never the raw token. Set both to different strong random secrets. Plaintext refresh tokens already in the database before an upgrade, as well as old tokens after changing SECRET_KEY, will fail validation, so users need to log in again.

docs.title: Registering authentication routes
docs.text:
Using register_all_auth_urls() is recommended: it initializes JWT and registers the login, registration, logout, email verification, and GitHub social login routes in one call:

from srf.auth.route import register_all_auth_urls

register_all_auth_urls(app, prefix="/api/auth")

JWT initialization reads and validates JWT_SECRET and SECRET_KEY from app.config, raising ServerError when either is missing.

If you only need a subset, compose the three fine-grained functions:

Function Registered endpoints register_jwt_urls(app, prefix) POST {prefix}/login, GET {prefix}/me, GET {prefix}/verify, POST {prefix}/refresh (sanic-jwt) register_auth_urls(instance, prefix) POST {prefix}/register, POST {prefix}/verify_email, POST {prefix}/logout register_social_auth_urls(instance, prefix) The three GitHub OAuth endpoints

Notes:

  • register_jwt_urls() only accepts a Sanic app instance. Initializing sanic-jwt on a Blueprint would attach ctx.auth to the blueprint, while the auth middleware reads request.app.ctx.auth and therefore would not find it.
  • None of these functions forward keyword arguments to sanic_jwt.Initialize. To customize sanic-jwt behavior (for example leeway or claim_iss), call sanic_jwt.Initialize directly.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
The default login endpoint is POST /api/auth/login. The request fields are account and password; account can be an email address or a username:

# Email login
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"account":"user@example.com","password":"password123"}'

Response (returned by sanic-jwt):

{
  "access_token": "******",
  "refresh_token": "******"
}

authenticate() uses UserLoginSchema (account, password), queries srf.auth.models.User, checks whether the user is enabled and verifies the password. sanic-jwt's build_payload() only puts user_id into the access token (plus exp); username and role names are returned by retrieve_user() on /me or refresh, and are never written into the token.

docs.title: Refreshing tokens
docs.text:
After the access token expires, exchange it for a new one by presenting the access token (expired is fine) together with the refresh token:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/auth/refresh \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <access-token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"refresh_token":"<refresh-token>"}'

The response contains only the new access_token; sanic-jwt does not rotate refresh tokens. Refresh tokens are persisted as HMAC digests with an absolute lifetime of JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRES (30 days by default); after expiry or logout the user must log in again.

Two other sanic-jwt endpoints: GET /api/auth/me returns the current user ({"me": {...}}), and GET /api/auth/verify checks token validity. Both are protected: a missing or invalid Authorization: Bearer header returns 401.

docs.title: Password and token algorithms
docs.text: SRF stores passwords as bcrypt(SHA-256(password)): the password is first encoded as UTF-8 and hashed with SHA-256, then bcrypt generates the password hash using a random salt. Login performs the same preprocessing and then verifies with bcrypt.checkpw().

docs.title: Authentication middleware
docs.text:
SRF ships a separate request middleware, set_user_to_request_ctx: it validates the Authorization: Bearer token and writes the user into request.ctx.user. By default (strict=False) authentication is optional — a request with no token falls back to AnonymousUser, while a presented-but-invalid token returns 401; strict=True enforces mandatory authentication. For the configuration example, whitelist filtering, and request flow, see Authentication Middleware.

This cleanly separates the semantics: 401 (authentication failure) comes from the middleware, 403 (authorization failure) from permission classes such as IsAuthenticated.

docs.title: Getting the current user
docs.text:
from sanic.response import json
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def create(self, request):
        user = self.get_current_user(request)
        if user is None or getattr(user, "is_anonymous", False):
            return json({"error": "Not logged in"}, status=401)
        # ...

get_current_user() returns request.ctx.user first, and falls back to request.auth when it does not exist.

docs.title: Registration and email verification codes
docs.text:
register_all_auth_urls() registers the following authentication routes (besides the four sanic-jwt JWT endpoints):

  • POST /api/auth/register
  • POST /api/auth/verify_email
  • POST /api/auth/logout

register issues tokens on success, so the application must already have called register_jwt_urls() (or register_all_auth_urls()). When JWT is not configured, the endpoint returns 500 and does not consume the verification code.

After USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_CODE_TIMES_LIMIT failed attempts the code is deleted and the endpoint returns 429 (TooManyRequest); the client must request a new verification code.

Email verification code settings are defined in srf.config.settings:

Option Default Purpose USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_VERIFY_CODE_TTL 60 Verification code lifetime in seconds USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_CODE USER_REGISTER:EMAIL_CODE:{email} Key format for the verification code in Redis; {email} is replaced with the email address USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_CODE_TIMES USER_REGISTER:EMAIL_CODE_TIMES:{email} Key format for the number of failed attempts in Redis USER_REGISTER_EMAIL_CODE_TIMES_LIMIT 10 Maximum allowed failed verification attempts

docs.title: Registration flow
docs.text:
# 1. Send the email verification code (repeated requests within the validity period return 429)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/auth/verify_email \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"user@example.com"}'

# 2. Read the 6-digit verification code from the email and submit the registration
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/auth/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"user@example.com","username":"zhangsan","password1":"Passw0rd123","password2":"Passw0rd123","confirmations":"123456"}'

# 3. Successful registration returns access_token / refresh_token; then access with the token
curl http://localhost:8000/api/users/self \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <access-token>"

# 4. Log out (revoke the current user's refresh token)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/auth/logout \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <access-token>"

docs.title: Registering the user resource API
docs.text:
register_all_auth_urls() only registers authentication flow routes and does not automatically register the user management resource. When you need the user profile and password change APIs, explicitly import UserViewSet and register it with SanicRouter:

from srf.auth.viewset import UserViewSet
from srf.route import SanicRouter

user_router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")
user_router.register("users", UserViewSet, name="users")

This resource provides GET /api/users/self, POST /api/users/change-password, POST /api/users/<user-id>/reset-password (superuser only), and the /api/users CRUD routes. Regular users can only access their own user record; superusers can manage other users. The password change request body is:

{
  "old_password": "old-password",
  "password1": "new-password",
  "password2": "new-password"
}

After a successful change, the user's saved refresh tokens are revoked; access tokens that have already been issued remain usable until they expire.

For the update endpoints (PUT/PATCH /api/users/<user-id>), submitting email, password, password1, or password2 returns 400. Changing the email address is not supported through this endpoint; password changes go only through the two dedicated endpoints: change-password for self-service (verifies the old password) and reset-password for superuser resets.

docs.title: User resource flow
docs.text:
# 1. Log in to get a token (account supports username or email)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"account":"user@example.com","password":"Passw0rd123"}'

# 2. Query your own profile
curl http://localhost:8000/api/users/self \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <access-token>"

# 3. Update your own profile
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/api/users/<user-id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <access-token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"new-name"}'

# 4. Change the password (log in again after success)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/users/change-password \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <access-token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"old_password":"Passw0rd123","password1":"NewPassw0rd456","password2":"NewPassw0rd456"}'

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Production environments must use HTTPS and read JWT_SECRET from a secret management system.
  • SRF enables refresh token persistence; logout revokes the current user's refresh token, but access tokens that have already been issued remain valid until they expire.
  • GitHub OAuth is an optional authentication feature; see the Social Login tutorial for configuration and integration.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text: SRF provides a flexible filtering system with search, query parameter filtering, and ordering capabilities.

docs.title: Filtering overview
docs.text:
The filtering system lets clients filter and sort data through query parameters and provides several built-in filters:

  • SearchFilter: Performs keyword search on configured fields
  • QueryParamFilter: Exact filtering based on query parameters
  • OrderingFactory: Sorting functionality

search_fields, filter_fields, and ordering_fields all default to an empty list []. All three accept either a list or a dictionary: field names in a list map to same-named ORM fields; a dictionary specifies ORM field names through its values, and the keys of filter_fields and ordering_fields are the request parameter names and available ordering names respectively. Use dictionaries when you need field aliases or ORM lookup expressions.

docs.title: BaseFilter
docs.text:
All filters inherit from the BaseFilter abstract base class:

from srf.filters.filter import BaseFilter


class BaseFilter:
    """Filter base class"""

    # Subclasses must set this: the name of the ViewSet attribute holding the field allowlist
    cls_fields: str | None = None

    def filter_queryset(self, request, queryset):
        """Filter the queryset

        Args:
            request: The request object
            queryset: The Tortoise ORM queryset

        Returns:
            The filtered queryset
        """
        raise NotImplementedError

BaseFilter.__init_subclass__() checks cls_fields: if a subclass forgets to set it, a TypeError is raised at class definition time. If you do not use a field allowlist, set it to "filter_fields" (or any existing ViewSet attribute name). filter_fields is normalized into {parameter name: ORM field name} when the filter is instantiated.

docs.title: SearchFilter - full-text search
docs.text:
SearchFilter gets search fields from search_fields and reads the search parameter from the request. Field names in a list and dictionary values are both treated as ORM field names.

class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    search_fields = ["name", "description", "sku"]
    # A dictionary is also supported, with ORM field names as values:
    # search_fields = {"product_name": "name", "product_description": "description"}

GET /api/products?search=phone
GET /api/products?search=wireless headphones

Multiple search fields are combined with OR; multiple keywords are combined with AND. In other words, the result must match every keyword, but each keyword may appear in any configured field.

docs.title: JsonLogicFilter - expression filtering
docs.text:
?filter= accepts a JSON Logic expression and can combine conditions within the filter_fields allowlist. Common operators include ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, in, not in, like (contains), and nested and / or / not are supported.

# Actual requests must URL-encode the JSON
GET /api/products?filter={"and":[{"==":[{"var":"is_active"},true]},{"like":[{"var":"name"},"phone"]}]}

Conditions on fields not present in filter_fields are ignored; if the JSON cannot be parsed, 400 is returned. See the Filters API for the complete operator table.

docs.title: QueryParamFilter - exact filtering
docs.text: QueryParamFilter performs exact matching based on query parameters.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    # Define the filter field mapping
    # A list is also supported, e.g. filter_fields = ["category_id", "is_active", ...]
    filter_fields = {
        "category": "category_id",       # Category ID
        "brand": "brand_id",             # Brand ID
        "is_active": "is_active",        # Whether active
        "min_price": "price__gte",       # Minimum price (greater than or equal)
        "max_price": "price__lte",       # Maximum price (less than or equal)
    }

docs.title: Request examples
docs.text:
# Filter by category
GET /api/products?category=1

# Price range filtering
GET /api/products?min_price=100&max_price=500

# Multiple conditions
GET /api/products?category=1&brand=2&min_price=100&is_active=true

docs.title: Mapping between filter_fields and query parameters
docs.text:
Query parameter names must exactly equal the keys of filter_fields. Lookup suffixes are written in the mapping's values, not in the query parameter names.

Lookup written in VALUE Tortoise Meaning filter_fields example Request (none) = Exact match "category": "category_id" ?category=1 __gte >= Greater than or equal "min_price": "price__gte" ?min_price=100 __lte <= Less than or equal "max_price": "price__lte" ?max_price=500 __gt > Greater than "min_stock": "stock__gt" ?min_stock=0 __lt < Less than "max_price_lt": "price__lt" ?max_price_lt=1000 __icontains ILIKE %x% Case-insensitive contains "name_contains": "name__icontains" ?name_contains=Phone __startswith LIKE x% Starts with "sku_starts": "sku__startswith" ?sku_starts=PRD

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    filter_fields = {
        # Exact match
        "category": "category_id",
        "status": "status",
        # Range queries
        "min_price": "price__gte",
        "max_price": "price__lte",
        "min_stock": "stock__gt",
        # Contains queries
        "name_contains": "name__icontains",
        "sku_starts": "sku__startswith",
        # Repeated parameters with the same name automatically get __in appended by QueryParamFilter
        "ids": "id",
        "categories": "category_id",
    }

Requests:

# Multiple IDs (repeated key → id__in)
GET /api/products?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3&ids=4&ids=5

# Multiple categories
GET /api/products?categories=1&categories=2&categories=3

# Name contains
GET /api/products?name_contains=phone

# SKU starts with
GET /api/products?sku_starts=PRD

# Price range (keys match filter_fields; the lookup is in the value)
GET /api/products?min_price=100&max_price=500

docs.title: OrderingFactory - ordering
docs.text: OrderingFactory provides sorting functionality.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    # A list maps field names to the same ORM field names
    # ordering_fields = ["price", "username", "created_at", "stock"]
    ordering_fields = {
        "price": "price",
        "name": "username",
        "created": "created_at",
        "stock": "stock",
    }

docs.title: Request examples
docs.text:
# Sort by price ascending
GET /api/products?ordering=price

# Sort by price descending (prefix with a minus sign)
GET /api/products?ordering=-price

# Sort by multiple fields
GET /api/products?ordering=-price,name

# Sort by category descending first, then by price ascending
GET /api/products?ordering=-category,price

docs.title: Ordering rules
docs.text:
• Ascending: the field name
  • Descending: prefix the field name with -
  • Multiple fields: separate with commas

docs.title: Combining filters
docs.text:
All filters can be used at the same time:

class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    # Define search fields
    search_fields = ["name", "description"]

    # Define filter fields
    filter_fields = {
        "category": "category_id",
        "min_price": "price__gte",
        "max_price": "price__lte",
        "is_active": "is_active",
    }

    # Define ordering fields
    ordering_fields = {
        "price": "price",
        "name": "name",
        "created": "created_at",
    }

docs.title: Combined query example
docs.text:
# Search + filter + order + paginate
GET /api/products?search=phone&category=1&min_price=1000&max_price=5000&ordering=-price&page=1&page_size=20

With the default filter_class, the execution order is:

  1. Apply search filtering (SearchFilter)
  2. Apply JSON Logic filtering (JsonLogicFilter)
  3. Apply exact filtering (QueryParamFilter)
  4. Apply ordering (OrderingFactory)
  5. Apply pagination (PageNumberPagination)

If the ViewSet customizes filter_class, the order of your custom list is used entirely.

docs.title: Creating a custom filter
docs.text:
from srf.filters.filter import BaseFilter
from tortoise.expressions import Q


class PriceRangeFilter(BaseFilter):
    """Price range filter"""

    # BaseFilter requires subclasses to declare cls_fields; this example does not read the allowlist, so any existing attribute name works
    cls_fields = "filter_fields"

    def filter_queryset(self, request, queryset):
        """Filter by price range (synchronous)"""
        price_range = request.args.get("price_range")

        if not price_range:
            return queryset

        # Parse the price range: "100-500"
        try:
            min_price, max_price = map(float, price_range.split("-"))
            queryset = queryset.filter(Q(price__gte=min_price) & Q(price__lte=max_price))
        except ValueError:
            pass

        return queryset

docs.title: Using a custom filter
docs.text:
from filters import PriceRangeFilter


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    filter_class = [
        PriceRangeFilter,
        SearchFilter,
        QueryParamFilter,
        OrderingFactory,
    ]

Request:

GET /api/products?price_range=100-500

docs.title: Combining filters in a custom action
docs.text:
filter_queryset() runs automatically in list(); custom actions need to construct filters manually:

from sanic.response import json


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    @action(methods=["get"], detail=False, url_path="popular")
    async def popular(self, request):
        queryset = Product.filter(is_active=True, stock__gt=0)

        # filter_queryset is synchronous; construct it with the ViewSet instance
        for filter_cls in [SearchFilter, OrderingFactory]:
            queryset = filter_cls(self).filter_queryset(request, queryset)

        products = await queryset.limit(10)
        results = [ProductSchemaReader.model_validate(p).model_dump() for p in products]
        return json({"results": results})

docs.title: 1. Add database indexes
docs.text:
Add indexes for commonly used filtering and ordering fields:

class Product(Model):
    category_id = fields.IntField(index=True)
    price = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2, index=True)
    created_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True, index=True)
    is_active = fields.BooleanField(default=True, index=True)

docs.title: 2. Limit search fields
docs.text:
Select only the necessary fields to avoid full table scans:

# Not recommended: searching too many fields
search_fields = ["name", "description", "content", "notes", "metadata"]

# Recommended: search only key fields
search_fields = ["name", "sku"]

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Choose filter fields sensibly: expose only the necessary filter fields
  2. Add database indexes: add indexes for filtering and ordering fields
  3. Limit search fields: avoid searching large text fields
  4. Validate input: validate the validity of filter parameters
  5. Combine filters: make full use of multiple filters together
  6. Document filter parameters: describe the supported filter parameters in the API documentation

docs.title: How do I implement date range queries?
docs.text:
class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    filter_fields = {
        "start_date": "created_at__gte",
        "end_date": "created_at__lte",
    }

GET /api/products?start_date=2026-01-01&end_date=2026-01-31

docs.title: How do I implement fuzzy search?
docs.text:
Use SearchFilter or QueryParamFilter:

# Option 1: SearchFilter
search_fields = ["name", "description"]

# Option 2: QueryParamFilter
filter_fields = {
    "name": "name__icontains",
}

docs.title: How do I disable a filter?
docs.text:
class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    # Use only some filters
    filter_class = [
        SearchFilter,
        QueryParamFilter,
        # Do not use OrderingFactory
    ]

docs.text:
• Study Pagination to learn how to combine it with filtering
  • Read Views for the complete functionality of ViewSets
  • See the Filters API for detailed API documentation

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text: SRF provides page-number-based pagination for list queries over large datasets.

docs.title: Pagination overview
docs.text: Pagination splits large datasets into multiple pages and returns only one page of data at a time, improving API performance and user experience.

docs.title: Main features
docs.text:
• Page-number based: uses a page number and page size for pagination
  • Automatic pagination: applied automatically in the ViewSet's list operation
  • Configurable: supports custom page sizes, maximum size limits, and other parameters
  • Unified response: returns a standardized paginated response format

docs.title: PageNumberPagination
docs.text: PageNumberPagination is SRF's pagination class. Custom pagination can inherit from BasePagination, in which case you must implement from_queryset(), paginate(), and num_pages(); or inherit from PageNumberPagination and override only the behavior you want to change. to_dict() already has a default implementation on BasePagination.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Pagination is applied automatically in BaseViewSet's list method:

from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    @property
    def queryset(self):
        return Product.all()

    def get_schema(self):
        return ProductSchemaReader if self.request.is_safe else ProductSchemaWriter

    # The list method applies pagination automatically

docs.title: Request examples
docs.text:
# Get page 1 with the default page size
GET /api/products?page=1

# Get page 2 with 20 items per page
GET /api/products?page=2&page_size=20

# The page parameter can be omitted on the first page
GET /api/products?page_size=10

docs.title: Response format
docs.text:
{
  "count": 100,
  "next": true,
  "previous": false,
  "results": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "name": "Product 1",
      "price": 99.99
    },
    {
      "id": 2,
      "name": "Product 2",
      "price": 89.99
    }
  ]
}

Field reference:

  • count: Total number of records
  • next: Whether there is a next page (boolean)
  • previous: Whether there is a previous page (boolean)
  • results: The list of data on the current page

docs.title: Default configuration
docs.text:
class PageNumberPagination:
    MAX_PAGE_SIZE: int = 100           # Upper bound for the requested page_size
    PAGE_QUERY_PARAM: str = 'page'     # Page number query parameter name
    PAGE_SIZE_QUERY_PARAM: str = 'page_size'  # Page size query parameter name

There are no page_size / max_page_size class attributes. In from_queryset(), non-integer page / page_size values fall back to defaults; values below 1 clamp to 1; and page_size is limited to at most MAX_PAGE_SIZE. Constructing PageNumberPagination directly applies the same range fixes.

docs.title: Creating a custom pagination class
docs.text:
from srf.paginator import PageNumberPagination


class CustomPagination(PageNumberPagination):
    MAX_PAGE_SIZE = 50
    PAGE_QUERY_PARAM = "p"
    PAGE_SIZE_QUERY_PARAM = "size"


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    pagination_class = CustomPagination

docs.title: Using pagination manually
docs.text:
Apply pagination manually in a custom action:

from srf.views import BaseViewSet
from srf.views.decorators import action
from srf.paginator import PageNumberPagination
from sanic.response import json


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    @action(methods=["get"], detail=False, url_path="featured")
    async def list_featured(self, request):
        """Get featured products (with pagination)"""
        # Get the queryset
        queryset = Product.filter(is_featured=True)

        # Create the paginator
        paginator = PageNumberPagination.from_queryset(queryset, request)

        # Get the schema
        schema = self.get_schema()

        # Paginate and serialize
        result = await paginator.to_dict(schema)

        return json(result)

docs.title: from_queryset(queryset, request)
docs.text:
Creates a paginator instance from a queryset and a request:

from srf.paginator import PageNumberPagination

# Create the paginator
paginator = PageNumberPagination.from_queryset(queryset=Product.all(), request=request)

docs.title: paginate(sch_model)
docs.text:
Performs pagination and returns a PaginationResult object:

from schemas import ProductSchemaReader

paginator = PageNumberPagination.from_queryset(queryset, request)
result = await paginator.paginate(sch_model=ProductSchemaReader)

# result is a PaginationResult object
print(result.count)      # Total count
print(result.next)       # Whether there is a next page
print(result.previous)   # Whether there is a previous page
print(result.results)    # Current page data (already serialized)

docs.title: to_dict(sch_model)
docs.text:
Performs pagination and returns a dictionary:

from schemas import ProductSchemaReader

paginator = PageNumberPagination.from_queryset(queryset, request)
result_dict = await paginator.to_dict(sch_model=ProductSchemaReader)

# result_dict is a dictionary
# {
#   "count": 100,
#   "next": true,
#   "previous": false,
#   "results": [...]
# }

docs.title: Combining pagination with filtering
docs.text:
Pagination is usually used together with filtering, search, and ordering:

class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    search_fields = ["name", "description"]
    filter_fields = {
        "category": "category_id",
        "min_price": "price__gte",
    }
    ordering_fields = {
        "price": "price",
        "name": "name",
    }

    # Request example:
    # GET /api/products?category=1&min_price=1000&ordering=-price&page=1&page_size=20
    # Default filter_class execution order:
    # 1. SearchFilter
    # 2. JsonLogicFilter
    # 3. QueryParamFilter
    # 4. OrderingFactory
    # 5. Pagination

docs.title: Example 1: Adding extra metadata
docs.text:
from srf.paginator import PageNumberPagination
from sanic.response import json


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def list(self, request):
        """Custom list method that adds extra information"""
        # Get the queryset and apply filtering
        queryset = self.queryset
        for filter_class in self.filter_class:
            queryset = filter_class(self).filter_queryset(request, queryset)

        # Paginate
        paginator = PageNumberPagination.from_queryset(queryset, request)
        schema = self.get_schema()
        result = await paginator.to_dict(schema)

        # Add extra information
        result["total_pages"] = (result["count"] + paginator.page_size - 1) // paginator.page_size
        result["current_page"] = paginator.page
        result["page_size"] = paginator.page_size

        return json(result)

Response:

{
  "count": 100,
  "next": true,
  "previous": false,
  "total_pages": 10,
  "current_page": 1,
  "page_size": 10,
  "results": [...]
}

docs.title: Example 2: Cursor pagination
docs.text:
For large datasets, you can implement cursor pagination:

from sanic.response import json


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    @action(methods=["get"], detail=False, url_path="cursor-list")
    async def cursor_list(self, request):
        """Use cursor pagination"""
        cursor = request.args.get("cursor", 0)  # The last ID of the previous page
        limit = int(request.args.get("limit", 20))

        # Query records greater than the cursor
        queryset = Product.filter(id__gt=cursor).limit(limit + 1)
        products = await queryset

        # Check whether there is a next page
        has_next = len(products) > limit
        if has_next:
            products = products[:limit]

        # Serialize
        results = [ProductSchemaReader.model_validate(p).model_dump() for p in products]

        # Return the result
        next_cursor = products[-1].id if products and has_next else None

        return json(
            {
                "results": results,
                "next_cursor": next_cursor,
                "has_next": has_next,
            }
        )

docs.title: Basic pagination
docs.text:
// Get page 1
fetch("/api/products?page=1&page_size=20")
  .then((res) => res.json())
  .then((data) => {
    console.log("Total:", data.count);
    console.log("Current page:", data.results);
    console.log("Has next page:", data.next);
  });

docs.title: Pagination navigation
docs.text:
let currentPage = 1;

async function loadPage(page) {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/products?page=${page}&page_size=20`);
  const data = await response.json();

  // Render the data
  renderProducts(data.results);

  // Update the navigation buttons
  document.getElementById("prev-btn").disabled = !data.previous;
  document.getElementById("next-btn").disabled = !data.next;

  currentPage = page;
}

// Previous page
document.getElementById("prev-btn").onclick = () => {
  if (currentPage > 1) {
    loadPage(currentPage - 1);
  }
};

// Next page
document.getElementById("next-btn").onclick = () => {
  loadPage(currentPage + 1);
};

docs.title: Infinite scrolling
docs.text:
let currentPage = 1;
let isLoading = false;
let hasMore = true;

async function loadMore() {
  if (isLoading || !hasMore) return;

  isLoading = true;

  const response = await fetch(
    `/api/products?page=${currentPage}&page_size=20`,
  );
  const data = await response.json();

  // Append data
  appendProducts(data.results);

  // Update state
  hasMore = data.next;
  currentPage++;
  isLoading = false;
}

// Listen for scrolling
window.addEventListener("scroll", () => {
  if (window.innerHeight + window.scrollY >= document.body.offsetHeight - 500) {
    loadMore();
  }
});

// Initial load
loadMore();

docs.title: 1. Use count() for optimization
docs.text:
For large datasets, use count() instead of len():

# Not recommended: loads all data
total = len(await Product.all())

# Recommended: only counts the records
total = await Product.all().count()

docs.title: 2. Use only() to select fields
docs.text:
Query only the fields you need:

@property
def queryset(self):
    # Only query the fields needed by the list
    return Product.all().only("id", "name", "price", "image")

docs.title: 3. Use prefetch_related to optimize related queries
docs.text:
@property
def queryset(self):
    # Preload related objects to reduce the number of queries
    return Product.all().prefetch_related("category", "brand")

docs.title: 4. Add indexes
docs.text:
Add database indexes for fields commonly used in filtering and ordering:

class Product(Model):
    name = fields.CharField(max_length=200, index=True)
    price = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2, index=True)
    created_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True, index=True)

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Choose a reasonable page size: 10-50 items is usually appropriate; avoid overly large values
  2. Limit the maximum page size: subclass and set MAX_PAGE_SIZE
  3. Combine with filtering: pagination should be used together with filtering, search, and ordering
  4. Optimize queries: use only(), prefetch_related(), and similar techniques to optimize queries
  5. Cache the total count: for data that rarely changes, you can cache the total count
  6. Add indexes: add database indexes for ordering and filtering fields
  7. Return metadata: return extra information such as the total page count and current page for client convenience

docs.title: How do I disable pagination?
docs.text: The built-in list() must use a pagination class (pagination_class = None causes list() to raise an error). For endpoints that should not paginate, override list() or add a custom action (see "Get all data" below).

docs.title: How do I get all data (without pagination)?
docs.text:
# page_size is limited by PageNumberPagination.MAX_PAGE_SIZE (default 100)
GET /api/products?page_size=100

Or add a custom action in the ViewSet:

@action(methods=["get"], detail=False, url_path="all")
async def get_all(self, request):
    """Get all products (without pagination)"""
    products = await Product.all()
    results = [ProductSchemaReader.model_validate(p).model_dump() for p in products]
    return json({"results": results})

docs.title: How do I implement offset/limit pagination?
docs.text:
@action(methods=["get"], detail=False, url_path="offset-list")
async def offset_list(self, request):
    """Use offset/limit pagination"""
    offset = int(request.args.get("offset", 0))
    limit = int(request.args.get("limit", 20))

    queryset = Product.all()
    total = await queryset.count()

    products = await queryset.offset(offset).limit(limit)

    results = [ProductSchemaReader.model_validate(p).model_dump() for p in products]

    return json(
        {
            "total": total,
            "offset": offset,
            "limit": limit,
            "results": results,
        }
    )

docs.text:
• Study Filtering to learn how to combine it with pagination
  • Read Views for the complete functionality of ViewSets
  • See Performance Optimization for more optimization techniques

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: SRF permission classes control access to ViewSets. View-level checks run before the handler through check_permissions(); object-level checks run when get_object() calls check_object_permissions() (covering retrieve / update / destroy, as well as custom actions that call get_object()).

docs.title: Built-in permission classes
docs.text:
from srf.permission.permission import (
    AllowAny,
    BasePermission,
    IsAuthenticated,
    SuperuserOnly,
    SafeMethodOnly,
)
  • AllowAny: Always allow (the default value of settings.DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES).
  • IsAuthenticated: request.ctx.user exists and the user's is_active is true.
  • SuperuserOnly: request.ctx.user.is_superuser is true.
  • SafeMethodOnly: Only GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are allowed.

Declare permission classes on a ViewSet:

from srf.permission.permission import IsAuthenticated
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class OrderViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    permission_classes = (IsAuthenticated,)

BaseViewSet.check_permissions() calls has_permission(request, view) on the class in order; both synchronous and asynchronous return values are supported. If any result is falsy, it raises 403 Forbidden. For the authentication middleware behavior (by default a request with no token falls back to AnonymousUser; strict=True enforces mandatory authentication), see Authentication Middleware; unauthenticated requests are decided by permission classes (IsAuthenticated rejects them with 403).

Permission methods are @staticmethods: inheriting from BasePermission is recommended but not required; providing a static method with the same name is enough (duck typing).

docs.title: Custom view-level permissions
docs.text:
from srf.permission.permission import BasePermission


class IsEditor(BasePermission):
    @staticmethod
    def has_permission(request, view=None):
        user = getattr(request.ctx, "user", None)
        # is_editor is an application-defined field; the built-in SRF User only has is_superuser and the roles relationship.
        return user is not None and getattr(user, "is_editor", False)

view is an optional parameter; BaseViewSet passes the current View instance.

Asynchronous checks work as well:

from models import Subscription
from srf.permission.permission import BasePermission


class HasActiveSubscription(BasePermission):
    @staticmethod
    async def has_permission(request, view=None):
        user = getattr(request.ctx, "user", None)
        return user is not None and await Subscription.filter(user_id=user.id, active=True).exists()

docs.title: Setting permissions by request method
docs.text:
To differentiate permissions by operation, select permission classes based on self.action in check_permissions():

import asyncio

from sanic.exceptions import Forbidden
from srf.permission.permission import IsAuthenticated, SuperuserOnly
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def check_permissions(self, request):
        if request.method.upper() in ("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
            return

        classes = (IsAuthenticated,) if request.method.upper() == "POST" else (IsAuthenticated, SuperuserOnly)
        for permission_class in classes:
            result = permission_class.has_permission(request, self)
            if asyncio.iscoroutine(result):
                result = await result
            if not result:
                raise Forbidden(message="Forbidden")

docs.title: Object-level permissions
docs.text:
BasePermission.has_object_permission(request, view, obj) defines the object-level interface. get_object() calls check_object_permissions(), which calls has_object_permission(request, view, obj) on the permission class and raises Forbidden when the result is falsy.

Object-level checks are not applied item by item to list results. List endpoints should limit data in the queryset.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from models import Order
from srf.permission.permission import BasePermission, IsAuthenticated
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class IsOwner(BasePermission):
    """Object-level permission: check whether the user is the owner"""

    @staticmethod
    def has_object_permission(request, view=None, obj=None):
        # Users can only view, modify, and delete their own objects
        return obj.owner_id == request.ctx.user.id


class OrderViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    permission_classes = (IsAuthenticated, IsOwner)

Limit visible data on the list side through queryset:

from models import Order
from srf.permission.permission import IsAuthenticated
from srf.views import BaseViewSet


class OrderViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    @property
    def queryset(self):
        user = self.get_current_user(self.request)
        if user.is_superuser:
            return Order.all()
        return Order.filter(user_id=user.id)

self.request is set by BaseViewSet.as_view() before handling the request.

docs.title: Permissions for custom actions
docs.text:
All actions registered by SanicRouter first run the ViewSet's check_permissions(). If additional restrictions are needed, perform extra checks inside the action:

from sanic.exceptions import Forbidden
from sanic.response import json
from models import Product
from srf.permission.permission import SuperuserOnly
from srf.views import BaseViewSet
from srf.views.decorators import action


class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    @action(methods=["post"], detail=True, url_path="approve")
    async def approve(self, request, pk):
        if not SuperuserOnly.has_permission(request, self):
            raise Forbidden(message="Superuser permission required")
        product = await self.get_object(pk)
        product.is_approved = True
        await product.save()
        return json({"message": "Approved"})

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Principle of least privilege: deny access by default and grant only the necessary permissions
  2. Separation of concerns: keep permission logic in dedicated permission classes
  3. Composing permissions: combine several simple permission classes to implement complex permissions
  4. Object-level permissions: use object-level permission checks for sensitive resources
  5. Async support: use asynchronous methods when database queries are needed
  6. Clear error messages: provide friendly permission error messages
  7. Test permissions: write unit tests for permission classes

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Authentication to learn about JWT authentication.
  • Read Authentication and Permissions Together for combined examples.
  • See Authentication Middleware to learn how request.ctx.user is set.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text: SRF's routing system automatically generates RESTful routes for ViewSets through the SanicRouter class.

docs.title: SanicRouter basics
docs.text:
SanicRouter is SRF's core routing class. It is responsible for:

  • Registering ViewSets as routes
  • Automatically generating standard RESTful endpoints
  • Discovering and registering custom actions decorated with @action
  • Managing URL prefixes and naming

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from sanic import Sanic
from srf.route import SanicRouter
from viewsets import ProductViewSet

app = Sanic("ShopApp")
router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")

# Register the ViewSet
router.register("products", ProductViewSet, name="products")

docs.title: SanicRouter(instance, prefix="")
docs.text:
router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")

Parameter reference:

  • instance: Required. A Sanic Sanic or Blueprint instance. When a Sanic instance is passed, routes are registered directly on the application; when a Blueprint is passed, routes are registered on that Blueprint.
  • prefix: URL prefix added in front of all routes

docs.title: register(path, view_cls, name=None)
docs.text:
router.register(
    path="products",           # URL path
    view_cls=ProductViewSet,   # ViewSet class
    name="products"            # Optional: route name
)

Parameter reference:

  • path: URL path of the resource (without the prefix)
  • view_cls: ViewSet class
  • name: Route name prefix used to generate route names

docs.title: Automatically generated routes
docs.text: When a ViewSet is registered, SanicRouter automatically generates the following routes:

docs.title: Standard CRUD routes
docs.text:
Assume the registration code is:

router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")
router.register("products", ProductViewSet, name="products")

Generated routes:

HTTP method URL path Operation ViewSet method Route name GET /api/products List list() products-list HEAD /api/products List (no body) list() products-list POST /api/products Create create() products-list GET /api/products/<pk> Detail retrieve() products-detail HEAD /api/products/<pk> Detail (no body) retrieve() products-detail PUT /api/products/<pk> Full update update() products-detail PATCH /api/products/<pk> Partial update update() products-detail DELETE /api/products/<pk> Delete destroy() products-detail

docs.title: Custom action routes
docs.text:
For methods decorated with @action:

Collection-level actions (detail=False):

@action(methods=["get"], detail=False, url_path="featured")
async def list_featured(self, request):
    pass

Generated route:

  • URL: /api/products/featured
  • Method: GET
  • Route name: products-list_featured (the default url_name is the method name)

Detail-level actions (detail=True):

@action(methods=["post"], detail=True, url_path="publish")
async def publish(self, request, pk):
    pass

Generated route:

  • URL: /api/products/<pk>/publish
  • Method: POST
  • Route name: products-publish (the default url_name is the method name)

docs.title: URL prefixes
docs.text: URL prefixes add a common prefix to all routes.

docs.title: A single prefix
docs.text:
router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")
router.register("products", ProductViewSet)
# Generated: /api/products, /api/products/<pk>

docs.title: Versioned APIs
docs.text:
# v1 API
router_v1 = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/v1")
router_v1.register("products", ProductViewSetV1)
# Generated: /api/v1/products

# v2 API
router_v2 = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/v2")
router_v2.register("products", ProductViewSetV2)
# Generated: /api/v2/products

docs.title: Nested resources
docs.text:
SanicRouter.register() appends collection and detail paths after the resource name. For nested routes, put the parent resource ID in the prefix and register the child resource name as path. The child resource ViewSet must limit its data by the parent resource ID in get_queryset():

review_router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/products/<product_id:int>")
review_router.register("reviews", ReviewViewSet)
# Collection: /api/products/<product_id:int>/reviews
# Detail: /api/products/<product_id:int>/reviews/<pk>

docs.title: Registering in the same router
docs.text:
router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")

# Register multiple ViewSets
router.register("products", ProductViewSet)
router.register("categories", CategoryViewSet)
router.register("orders", OrderViewSet)
router.register("reviews", ReviewViewSet)

docs.title: Using multiple routers
docs.text:
# Public API routes
public_router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/public")
public_router.register("products", ProductViewSet)
public_router.register("categories", CategoryViewSet)

# Admin API routes
admin_router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/admin")
admin_router.register("users", UserViewSet)
admin_router.register("orders", OrderViewSet)

docs.title: Custom Blueprints
docs.text:
When you need to organize routes by module or add Blueprint middleware to routes, you can pass your own Blueprint object. SanicRouter registers routes directly on that Blueprint; after registration, mount the Blueprint on the Sanic application with app.blueprint(bp). The URL prefix is set uniformly through SanicRouter's prefix:

from sanic import Blueprint
from srf.route import SanicRouter

# Create a custom Blueprint
my_blueprint = Blueprint("my_api")

# Use the custom Blueprint
router = SanicRouter(my_blueprint, prefix="api")
router.register("products", ProductViewSet)

# After the Blueprint has completed route registration, mount it on the Sanic application
app.blueprint(my_blueprint)

docs.title: URL reverse resolution
docs.text:
Generate URLs using route names:

from sanic import Sanic

app = Sanic("MyApp")

# ... register routes ...

# Reverse resolve a URL
url = app.url_for("products-list")
# Result: /api/products

url = app.url_for("products-detail", pk=1)
# Result: /api/products/1

url = app.url_for("products-list_featured")
# Result: /api/products/featured

url = app.url_for("products-publish", pk=1)
# Result: /api/products/1/publish

Using it in a ViewSet:

class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def create(self, request):
        # ... create the product ...

        # Generate the detail URL
        detail_url = request.app.url_for("products-detail", pk=product.id)

        return json({"id": product.id, "url": detail_url}, status=201)

docs.title: Route middleware
docs.text:
Add middleware for specific routes:

from sanic import Blueprint
from srf.route import SanicRouter

# Create a Blueprint
bp = Blueprint("api")


# Add middleware
@bp.middleware("request")
async def add_custom_header(request):
    request.ctx.custom_data = "value"


# Use the Blueprint
router = SanicRouter(bp, prefix="api")
router.register("products", ProductViewSet)

app.blueprint(bp)

docs.title: Example 1: Basic route setup
docs.text:
# app.py
from sanic import Sanic
from srf.route import SanicRouter
from viewsets import ProductViewSet, CategoryViewSet

app = Sanic("ShopApp")

# Create the router
router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api")

# Register ViewSets
router.register("products", ProductViewSet, name="products")
router.register("categories", CategoryViewSet, name="categories")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

Generated routes:

GET    /api/products              -> list
POST   /api/products              -> create
GET    /api/products/<pk>         -> retrieve
PUT    /api/products/<pk>         -> update
PATCH  /api/products/<pk>         -> update
DELETE /api/products/<pk>         -> destroy

GET    /api/categories            -> list
POST   /api/categories            -> create
GET    /api/categories/<pk>       -> retrieve
PUT    /api/categories/<pk>       -> update
PATCH  /api/categories/<pk>       -> update
DELETE /api/categories/<pk>       -> destroy

docs.title: Example 2: Multi-version API
docs.text:
# routes.py
from srf.route import SanicRouter
from viewsets.v1 import ProductViewSetV1
from viewsets.v2 import ProductViewSetV2


def register_routes(app):
    # v1 routes
    router_v1 = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/v1")
    router_v1.register("products", ProductViewSetV1)

    router_v2 = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/v2")
    router_v2.register("products", ProductViewSetV2)

Generated routes:

# v1 API
GET    /api/v1/products           -> ProductViewSetV1.list
POST   /api/v1/products           -> ProductViewSetV1.create
GET    /api/v1/products/<pk>      -> ProductViewSetV1.retrieve

# v2 API
GET    /api/v2/products           -> ProductViewSetV2.list
POST   /api/v2/products           -> ProductViewSetV2.create
GET    /api/v2/products/<pk>      -> ProductViewSetV2.retrieve

docs.title: Viewing all routes
docs.text:
@app.before_server_start
async def print_routes(app, loop):
    """Print all registered routes"""
    for route in app.router.routes:
        print(f"{route.methods} {route.path} -> {route.name}")

docs.title: Using Sanic's route list
docs.text:
from sanic import Sanic

app = Sanic("MyApp")
# ... register routes ...

# Print routes
for route in app.router.routes:
    methods = ", ".join(route.methods)
    print(f"[{methods}] {route.path}")

Example output:

[GET, HEAD, POST] /api/products
[GET, HEAD, PUT, PATCH, DELETE] /api/products/<pk>
[GET] /api/products/featured
[POST] /api/products/<pk>/publish

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Use meaningful path names: paths should clearly indicate the resource type
  2. Keep URL structure consistent: use a consistent naming convention
  3. Version APIs: use URL prefixes to distinguish versions
  4. Modular organization: organize related routes together
  5. Use route names: leverage route names for URL reverse resolution
  6. Document routes: add docstrings to each ViewSet

docs.title: How do I disable certain HTTP methods?
docs.text:
Override the corresponding method and return a 405 error:

class ProductViewSet(BaseViewSet):
    async def destroy(self, request, pk):
        """Disable the delete operation"""
        from sanic.response import json

        return json({"error": "Delete operations are not supported"}, status=405)

docs.title: How do I customize URL parameter types?
docs.text:
Use Sanic's path parameter syntax:

# The pk parameter generated by SanicRouter does not specify a type; SRF normalizes the primary key when get_object(pk) is called
# /api/products/<pk>

# Other types can be used in custom actions
@action(methods=["get"], detail=True, url_path="by-slug/<slug:str>")
async def get_by_slug(self, request, pk, slug):
    pass

docs.title: How do I handle nested resources?
docs.text:
Use multiple routers with different URL prefixes:

# Product routes
router.register("products", ProductViewSet)

# Reviews under products (product_id must be handled in the ViewSet)
review_router = SanicRouter(app, prefix="api/products/<product_id:int>")
review_router.register("reviews", ReviewViewSet)

docs.text:
